CursorBench tasks necessitate substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7–10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. At the same time, CursorBench prompts are also more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185–3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the structural differences between CursorBench and public benchmarks?
choices: CursorBench has 181 median lines changed and 390 character prompts
CursorBench has 65 median lines changed and 500 character prompts
CursorBench has 7 median lines changed and 1,185 character prompts
CursorBench has 10 median lines changed and 3,055 character prompts
questions.explanation: CursorBench tasks require substantially more code changes (median 181 lines) compared to public benchmarks (7-10 lines), while having much shorter prompt descriptions (390 characters vs 1,185-3,055 characters).

questions.lessonContent: To run evaluations during Composer 2 training, the system follows a specific deployment process. First, for each training step we want to evaluate, we must acquire an evaluation deployment lease to reserve the necessary resources. Once the lease is acquired, the system automatically moves GPUs to that deployment to enable inference. Finally, we perform a cross-region weight sync of the evaluation checkpoint from the training cluster where it resides to the inference deployment. This ensures the evaluation uses the exact model weights from the current training step.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 evaluation deployment process?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo (or wherever you run claude from), which is the most common usage; any parent of the directory where you run claude, which is most useful for monorepos; any child of the directory where you run claude, where Claude will pull in CLAUDE.md files on demand when working with files in child directories; and your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies it to all your claude sessions. You can name it CLAUDE.md and check it into git to share across sessions and with your team, or name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it.
questions.question: Where can you place CLAUDE.md files?
questions.answer: The root of your repo (or wherever you run claude from), any parent directory, any child directory, or your home folder (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md)

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code is designed with a deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety. By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. This conservative default ensures that potentially destructive actions require explicit user approval before execution.
questions.question: Claude Code requests permission by default for actions that might modify your system.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code provides four ways to manage allowed tools. First, you can select "Always allow" when prompted during a session. Second, you can use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist, such as adding Edit to always allow file edits or Bash(git commit:*) to allow git commits. Third, you can manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, with the former recommended for checking into source control to share with your team. Fourth, you can use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Which method for managing allowed tools involves using the /permissions command?
choices: Select "Always allow" when prompted during a session
Use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions
Use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools
questions.explanation: The /permissions command is specifically mentioned as a way to add or remove tools from the allowlist after starting Claude Code, such as adding Edit for file edits or Bash(git commit:*) for git commits.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code inherits your bash environment, giving it access to all your standard tools like unix utilities and the gh CLI. However, Claude won't automatically know about your custom bash tools without explicit instructions. To add custom tools, you should tell Claude the tool name with usage examples, instruct Claude to run the --help flag to see tool documentation, and document frequently used tools in your CLAUDE.md file for future reference.
questions.question: What three steps should you follow to help Claude understand your custom bash tools?
questions.answer: Tell Claude the tool name with usage examples, tell Claude to run --help to see tool documentation, and document frequently used tools in CLAUDE.md

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, allowing it to connect to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. MCP servers can be configured in three ways: in project config when running Claude Code in a specific directory, in global config to make them available in all projects, or in a checked-in .mcp.json file that makes tools available to anyone working in your codebase.
questions.question: Claude Code can connect to MCP servers through three configuration methods. Is it possible to have MCP tools available to everyone working on a repository without requiring individual setup?

questions.lessonContent: Many Anthropic engineers use Claude for over 90% of their git interactions. Claude can search git history to answer questions about changes, such as what went into a specific version or who owns a particular feature. It can also compose commit messages by automatically looking at your changes and recent history. Additionally, Claude can handle complex git operations including reverting files, resolving rebase conflicts, and comparing and grafting patches.
questions.question: Which of the following git operations can Claude Code perform?
choices: Modifying commit timestamps to alter project history
Creating new git branches without user confirmation
Searching git history to understand why certain decisions were made
questions.explanation: Claude can search git history to answer questions about changes and understand design decisions. The other options are either not supported or would be unsafe operations that Claude would not perform without explicit permission.

questions.lessonContent: The "Explore, plan, code, commit" workflow is a versatile pattern that suits many problems. First, ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs, providing either general pointers or specific filenames, but explicitly tell it not to write any code just yet. Next, ask Claude to make a plan for how to approach a specific problem, using the word "think" to trigger extended thinking mode for additional computation time. Third, ask Claude to implement its solution in code, and ask it to explicitly verify the reasonableness of its solution as it implements pieces. Finally, ask Claude to commit the result and create a pull request, and have it update any READMEs or changelogs with an explanation of what it just did.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the "Explore, plan, code, commit" workflow?
choices: Ask Claude to plan the approach
Ask Claude to read relevant files
Ask Claude to implement the code

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees for Parallel Claude Sessions
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, providing a lighter-weight alternative to having multiple git checkouts in separate folders. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. Using git worktrees enables you to run multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project, each focused on its own independent task. For example, you might have one Claude refactoring your authentication system while another builds a completely unrelated data visualization component. Since the tasks don't overlap, each Claude can work at full speed without waiting for the other's changes or dealing with merge conflicts.
questions.question: What is the key advantage of using git worktrees over having multiple git checkouts in separate folders?
questions.answer: Git worktrees are lighter-weight and allow checking out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories while sharing the same Git history and reflog

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. You can use the -p flag with a prompt to enable headless mode, and --output-format stream-json for streaming JSON output. However, a critical limitation to understand is that headless mode does not persist between sessions—you have to trigger it each session. This means every time you want to run Claude in headless mode, you must explicitly invoke it with the -p flag rather than having it carry over from a previous session.
questions.question: Headless mode in Claude Code persists between sessions once activated.

questions.lessonContent: Beyond standalone usage, some of the most powerful applications involve running multiple Claude instances in parallel. One approach is to have one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it—similar to working with multiple engineers. Another approach is using multiple git checkouts in separate folders, where you open each folder in separate terminal tabs and start Claude in each folder with different tasks, then cycle through to check progress and approve or deny permission requests. A third approach uses git worktrees for multiple independent tasks, which offers a lighter-weight alternative to multiple checkouts.
questions.question: Which multi-instance workflow approach is described as the lightest-weight alternative to multiple git checkouts?
choices: Having one Claude write code while another verifies
Running Claude in headless mode with a custom harness
Using multiple git checkouts in separate folders
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that git worktrees 'shine for multiple independent tasks, offering a lighter-weight alternative to multiple checkouts.'

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: An HD screenshot with dimensions 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels. Each pixel stores three color values representing red, green, and blue intensity, with each value ranging from 0 (indicating no color) to 255 (indicating maximum color intensity). Since each color requires one byte of storage, a single pixel needs 3 bytes. Multiplying these together gives 2,073,600 × 3 bytes = 6,220,800 bytes, which is approximately 6.2 megabytes for a single uncompressed HD image. This large file size demonstrates why compression techniques are essential for storing and transmitting images efficiently.
questions.question: How many pixels does a 1920 × 1080 HD image contain?

questions.lessonTitle: The Two Fundamental Approaches to Compression
questions.lessonContent: There are two primary approaches to image compression that form the foundation of all modern image formats. The first approach, lossy compression, involves throwing away data that humans are unlikely to notice, trading some quality for significantly smaller file sizes. The second approach, lossless compression, uses clever methods to store every pixel perfectly while still reducing file size through efficiency tricks. These two fundamental ideas respectively power formats like JPEG for lossy compression and PNG for lossless compression, as well as other technologies like ZIP files and web traffic. Understanding the distinction between these approaches is essential for choosing the right compression method for different use cases.
questions.question: Lossy compression preserves every original pixel while lossless compression does not.

questions.lessonContent: Digital images appear smooth and continuous but are actually constructed from tiny colored squares called pixels that form a grid. Each pixel contains three numerical values specifying how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create its final color. These three values each range from 0, representing the absence of that color, to 255, representing the maximum intensity of that color. By combining different intensities of these three primary colors, pixels can represent millions of different colors across the visible spectrum. For example, a pixel with values rgb(255, 147, 41) would appear orange due to high red, moderate green, and low blue values.
questions.question: What three color values make up each pixel in a digital image?
questions.explanation: Each pixel stores three values representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together, with each value ranging from 0 to 255.

questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression (used by PNG) preserves every single pixel while still shrinking the file. PNG combines three key tricks in sequence. First, Filtering stores differences between adjacent pixels rather than absolute values. Next, LZ77 finds repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with compact back-references. Finally, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to the most common values. The result is a significantly smaller file without any loss in image quality.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG compression pipeline?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Perception
questions.lessonTitle: JPEG Block Processing in Image Compression
questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides images into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients in the image, while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG exploits this by throwing away the high-frequency details that humans won't notice, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: What is the size of the pixel blocks that JPEG divides an image into for processing?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Perception
questions.lessonContent: The human visual system has specific limitations that lossy compression algorithms exploit. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. You notice a blurry edge in an image, but you won't notice if colors are slightly off. JPEG takes advantage of this by converting pixels from RGB to a format that separates brightness from color, then reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice the difference.
questions.question: According to the content, human eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Perception
questions.lessonContent: JPEG uses a clever approach to compress images by separating brightness from color information. When processing an image, JPEG converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates luminance from chrominance. This allows the algorithm to reduce color resolution significantly while maintaining the visual quality that human perception requires, since our eyes are more sensitive to brightness changes than color changes.
questions.question: What does JPEG convert pixels from to separate brightness from color?
questions.explanation: The content states that JPEG converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. This transformation allows JPEG to reduce color resolution since human eyes are less sensitive to color detail than brightness detail.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG Pipeline and Algorithms
questions.lessonContent: PNG uses filtering or prediction to compress images by storing differences between adjacent pixels rather than storing each pixel value directly. Instead of storing values like 128, 130, 132, 134, PNG stores only how much each pixel differs from its neighbor. PNG supports four prediction methods: Sub predicts from the left neighbor (best for horizontal gradients), Up predicts from the pixel above (best for vertical gradients), Average predicts from the average of left and above, and Paeth smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal. PNG encoders try each method per row and pick the one that compresses best.
questions.question: What are the four prediction methods used in PNG compression?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG Pipeline and Algorithms
questions.lessonContent: After filtering, the data might contain repeated patterns like 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2... A clever algorithm called LZ77 spots these patterns and replaces them with back-references. Instead of storing the same sequence twice, LZ77 says "go back 5 values and copy 5." This tiny reference is smaller than repeating the values. LZ77 maintains a "sliding window" of the last 32 KB of data, and any pattern within that window can be referenced instead of repeated. This technique helps reduce file size significantly for images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients.
questions.question: LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data to find repeated patterns.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG Pipeline and Algorithms
questions.lessonContent: PNG and JPEG handle transparency differently due to their compression approaches. JPEG uses lossy compression that exploits how human vision works by grouping nearby pixels and averaging colors, which is incompatible with preserving precise alpha transparency values. PNG uses lossless compression that preserves every single pixel perfectly, including a fourth channel called alpha that represents transparency. While standard RGB uses 3 bytes per pixel (red, green, blue), RGBA uses 4 bytes per pixel to include the alpha channel. This makes PNG the preferred format for graphics that require transparency, such as logos, icons, and web elements with transparent backgrounds.
questions.question: Which format supports alpha (transparency) channel: PNG or JPEG?
questions.explanation: PNG supports alpha (transparency) as a fourth channel, using 4 bytes per pixel instead of 3. JPEG does not support alpha, which is why PNG is preferred for graphics with transparency.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG Pipeline and Algorithms
questions.lessonTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG Pipeline and Algorithms
questions.lessonContent: PNG uses three main compression tricks in sequence to shrink image files while preserving every pixel. First, filtering predicts each pixel from its neighbors and stores the differences instead of raw values, which are typically small numbers. Second, LZ77 pattern finding scans for repeated sequences in the last 32 KB of data and replaces them with compact back-references. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to frequently occurring values (like 0, which might appear 60% of the time) and longer codes to rare values. Finally, the compressed data gets wrapped in PNG format with headers and checksums.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the three main compression techniques used in PNG lossless compression?

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images appear smooth and continuous to the human eye, but when zoomed in significantly, they reveal a granular structure composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numerical values representing color channels: red, green, and blue. Each color value ranges from 0, indicating the absence of that color, to 255, representing maximum intensity of that color. For example, the RGB value rgb(255, 147, 41) creates an orange hue with maximum red, moderate green, and low blue. These three values combine to produce the full spectrum of colors visible in digital images.
questions.question: What range of values does each color channel (red, green, blue) use in a pixel?

questions.lessonContent: Data compression is fundamental to how computers function, serving as the foundation for the internet, file systems, and most software applications. There exist exactly two primary approaches to compression: lossy compression, which discards data that humans are unlikely to notice, and lossless compression, which preserves every pixel through clever storage techniques. These two fundamental approaches power widely-used formats including JPEG, PNG, and ZIP files, as well as web traffic and much of the internet's infrastructure. The distinction between these approaches determines both file size and image quality.
questions.question: The two fundamental approaches to image compression are lossy and lossless compression.

questions.lessonContent: Understanding file sizes requires knowing how many pixels an image contains and how much data each pixel requires. A high-definition screenshot with dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels, specifically calculated as 1,920 multiplied by 1,080 equaling 2,073,600 pixels. Since each pixel needs 3 bytes to store its red, green, and blue values, the total file size equals 2,073,600 multiplied by 3 bytes, which equals 6,220,800 bytes, approximately 6.2 megabytes. This calculation demonstrates why uncompressed image files become very large and why compression is necessary for efficient storage and transmission.
questions.question: How many megabytes (approximately) does a single uncompressed 1920 × 1080 pixel image require?
questions.explanation: The calculation shows 1,920 × 1,080 = 2,073,600 pixels, and 2,073,600 × 3 bytes = 6,220,800 bytes, which equals approximately 6.2 MB.

questions.lessonContent: The PNG lossless compression pipeline uses three key techniques in sequence. First, Filtering stores differences between pixels rather than raw values, making the data more uniform. Second, LZ77 Pattern Finding identifies repeated sequences in the data and replaces them with compact references. Third, Huffman Coding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values, further reducing file size.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: Into what size blocks does JPEG divide the image for processing?

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression (used by JPEG) exploits how human vision works. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. You notice a blurry edge, but you won't notice if colors are slightly off. With lossy compression, you can't get the original pixels back. The tradeoff is often worth it: 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference.
questions.question: With lossy compression, you can recover the exact original pixel values by decompressing the file.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG takes advantage of human vision characteristics in a clever way. First, it converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. It also reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss.
questions.question: Which aspect of human vision does JPEG primarily exploit for compression?
choices: Eyes see only red, green, and blue wavelengths
Eyes cannot detect any color changes
Eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together
questions.explanation: JPEG exploits the fact that human eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together, allowing color resolution to be reduced without noticeable quality loss.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression uses several key steps to shrink image files. First, it converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. It also reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice. Then it divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components using DCT. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the JPEG lossy compression pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses prediction methods to reduce file size by storing differences between pixels rather than absolute values. Instead of storing each value directly, PNG predicts each pixel based on its neighbors and only stores how wrong that prediction was. There are four main prediction methods: Sub (predicts from the left neighbor, best for horizontal gradients), Up (predicts from the pixel above, best for vertical gradients), Average (predicts from the average of left and above), and Paeth (smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal). PNG encoders try each method per row and select the one that compresses best for that particular row of data.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method is best for horizontal gradients?

questions.lessonContent: After prediction filtering, PNG uses the LZ77 algorithm to find repeated patterns in the data. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data it has processed. When it finds a pattern that has appeared before within this window, it replaces the repeated sequence with a back-reference that says go back a certain number of values and copy a certain number of values. This reference is much smaller than repeating the actual values. For images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients, this technique significantly reduces file size because the algorithm can reference previously encoded data instead of storing it again.
questions.question: The LZ77 algorithm in PNG uses a sliding window of 32 KB to find and reference repeated patterns.

questions.lessonContent: After filtering and LZ77 pattern-finding, some values appear much more frequently than others in the data. For example, the value 0 (representing no difference between predicted and actual pixel values) might appear 60% of the time, while 127 might appear only 5% of the time. Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to more common values and longer codes to rarer ones. Specifically, the value 0 gets just 1 bit (0), the value 2 gets 2 bits (10), values like 255 get 3 bits (110), and rare values like 127 get 3 bits (111). This approach mirrors Morse code, where common letters have short codes and rare letters have long codes.
questions.question: According to the source, what binary code does Huffman coding assign to the value 0 (which appears 60% of the time)?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that the value 0 (appears 60%) gets just 1 bit: 0. This is the shortest code because it is the most frequently occurring value after filtering.

questions.lessonContent: In lossless PNG compression, after gathering raw pixel data, the encoder tests multiple prediction methods to determine which one will compress best for each row. First, it tests prediction methods including Sub (predict from left neighbor), Up (predict from above), Average, and Paeth. Then, it selects best per row for each row of the image. Finally, it applies filtering by storing the differences between actual pixel values and predicted values, rather than storing the raw values themselves.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG prediction and filtering phase?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Our Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information and then returning findings to the lead agent so it can compile a final answer. This architecture differs from traditional Retrieval Augmented Generation approaches that use static retrieval, as the multi-agent system dynamically finds relevant information, adapts to new findings, and analyzes results to formulate high-quality answers.
questions.question: What architectural pattern does Anthropic's Research system use for coordinating multiple agents?

questions.lessonTitle: Multi-Agent Systems Enable Dynamic Research Approaches
questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems help solve problems that require flexibility because research demands the ability to pivot or explore tangential connections as the investigation unfolds. Traditional approaches using Retrieval Augmented Generation use static retrieval that fetches a fixed set of chunks most similar to an input query. In contrast, multi-agent architectures use multi-step search that dynamically finds relevant information and adapts to new findings. The model must operate autonomously for many turns, making decisions about which directions to pursue based on intermediate findings. A linear, one-shot pipeline cannot handle these dynamic, path-dependent tasks.
questions.question: Multi-agent research systems use dynamic, adaptive search rather than static retrieval methods.

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage Comparison in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. This higher token usage is a downside that requires tasks where the value is high enough to pay for the increased performance. Multi-agent architectures effectively scale token usage for tasks that exceed the limits of single agents. The architecture distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. Some domains that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today.
questions.question: Based on the source content, how many times more tokens do multi-agent systems use compared to standard chat interactions?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats, while single agents use about 4× more tokens than chats.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Effort to Query Complexity in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: In multi-agent research systems, agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so scaling rules must be embedded in the prompts. Simple fact-finding tasks require just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls. Direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 tool calls each. Complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions of the system.
questions.question: According to the source content, what is the recommended number of subagents and tool calls needed for a direct comparison task?

questions.lessonTitle: Starting Evaluations Early in Agent Development
questions.lessonContent: In early agent development, changes tend to have dramatic impacts because there is abundant low-hanging fruit. A prompt tweak might boost success rates from 30% to 80%. With effect sizes this large, you can spot changes with just a few test cases. Teams often delay creating evaluations because they believe only large evals with hundreds of test cases are useful. However, it is best to start with small-scale testing right away with a few examples representing real usage patterns, rather than delaying until more thorough evaluations can be built.
questions.question: Starting agent evaluations with small samples is ineffective and should be delayed until large evals can be built.

questions.lessonTitle: Evaluation Criteria for Research Agent Outputs
questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. LLMs are a natural fit for grading outputs. An LLM judge evaluates each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (whether claims match sources), citation accuracy (whether cited sources match the claims), completeness (whether all requested aspects are covered), source quality (whether it used primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources), and tool efficiency (whether it used the right tools a reasonable number of times).
questions.question: Which evaluation criterion checks whether the research output used primary sources rather than lower-quality secondary sources?
questions.explanation: The source quality criterion specifically evaluates whether the agent used primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources, such as preferring academic PDFs over SEO-optimized content farms.

questions.lessonContent: When evaluating multi-agent research systems, the recommended approach starts by testing prompts immediately with small samples, since in early agent development changes tend to have dramatic impacts and a prompt tweak might boost success rates dramatically with just a few test cases. After initial testing, LLM-as-judge evaluation is applied to scale the evaluation process, as research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically and LLMs provide a natural fit for grading outputs against criteria like factual accuracy and completeness. Finally, human evaluation is conducted to catch edge cases that automated evals miss, such as hallucinated answers on unusual queries or subtle source selection biases. This sequence ensures that refinements can be made based on findings before reaching a final validated research output.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the evaluation process for multi-agent research systems?

questions.lessonContent: In traditional software, a bug might break a feature or cause outages, but in agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes. Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls, which means errors compound significantly. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents. When errors occur, restarting from the beginning is expensive and frustrating for users. Instead, systems must be built that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred. We also use the model's intelligence to handle issues gracefully by letting the agent know when a tool is failing and letting it adapt.
questions.question: What approach does the source content recommend for handling errors in stateful agent systems instead of restarting from the beginning?
questions.answer: Building systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever we deploy updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. We therefore need to prevent our well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. We cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, we use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: Rainbow deployments allow all agents to be updated to new versions simultaneously for consistency.

questions.lessonContent: Currently, our lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination, but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. For instance, the lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. Asynchronous execution would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed. However, this asynchronicity adds challenges in result coordination, state consistency, and error propagation across the subagents.
questions.question: What are the current limitations of synchronous execution in multi-agent systems?
choices: The system fails to properly evaluate end-state outcomes
The agents cannot maintain state across multiple tool calls
The system uses too many tokens and becomes economically unviable
The lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that synchronous execution creates bottlenecks where the lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching.

questions.lessonContent: In the production system, when a user submits a query, the lead agent first analyzes the query to understand what information is needed. The lead agent then spawns specialized subagents to explore different aspects of the question in parallel. Each subagent executes its research task, and the lead agent waits for each subagent to complete before synthesizing all findings together. Finally, the consolidated results are returned to the user.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent research execution workflow?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers 8 open source embedding models that achieve state-of-the-art performance in MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark), showing comparable or even better accuracies than closed models. These include top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models. According to the source content, these models outperform OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3 in both MTEB and LoCo Benchmarks.
questions.question: Which two companies' embedding models do Together Embeddings models outperform in MTEB and LoCo Benchmarks?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides M2-BERT retrieval models specifically designed for long context tasks. These models are available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k. According to the source content, these M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks, enabling users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while maintaining more meaningful contexts in the embeddings.
questions.question: M2-BERT retrieval models are available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint can be used for various applications including data visualization. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model specifically, the embedding dimension is 768. When visualizing embeddings, the dimension is typically too large to plot directly, so tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) is used to transform the high-dimensional embedding vectors into a lower-dimensional space suitable for visualization.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?
questions.explanation: According to the source content, for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768.

questions.lessonTitle: OpenAI API Compatibility for Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing developers who have already built applications using the OpenAI API to easily switch to Together's service. To migrate, users simply need to configure their OpenAI client with a different base URL pointing to Together's API endpoint. The base URL for the Together Embeddings endpoint is "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings", and users must provide their Together API key when initializing the client. This compatibility feature significantly reduces the migration effort and allows for seamless integration into existing projects.
questions.question: What is the base URL for the Together Embeddings endpoint when using OpenAI API compatibility?

questions.lessonContent: Building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system with Together Embeddings provides flexibility through support for multiple popular vector databases and frameworks. Users can construct RAG systems using Together API alongside MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma for vector storage and retrieval. Additionally, the platform integrates with LangChain and LlamaIndex frameworks, which simplify the process of building RAG applications. The documentation provides detailed tutorials for implementing RAG with each of these tools, making it accessible for developers regardless of their preferred tech stack.
questions.question: True or False: Pinecone is mentioned as a vector database option for building RAG systems with Together Embeddings.

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings offers significant cost advantages compared to other popular embedding platforms. According to the documentation, the pricing is up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms, making it a cost-effective choice for organizations scaling their embedding-based applications. This pricing structure applies to all eight embedding models available through the platform, including the M2-BERT retrieval models for long context and the top models from the MTEB leaderboard. The cost efficiency, combined with the OpenAI-compatible API and framework integrations, makes Together an attractive option for developers building RAG systems and embedding applications.
questions.question: Which pricing claim is explicitly stated for Together Embeddings compared to other platforms?
choices: Up to 2x cheaper than other popular platforms
Up to 5x cheaper than other popular platforms
Up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms
Up to 3x cheaper than other popular platforms

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint can visualize sample data from various domains of RedPajama-v1 Sample. The code example in the documentation processes five different data files: arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, github_sample.jsonl, and stackexchange_sample.jsonl. Each of these represents a different domain or source of text data. When the embeddings are visualized using t-SNE, texts from each data source appear somewhat closely located together, showing that the embedding model successfully captures the semantic similarities within the same domain.
questions.question: Which five data source files are used in the code example for visualizing embeddings?
questions.answer: arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, github_sample.jsonl, and stackexchange_sample.jsonl

questions.lessonContent: Embedding vectors typically have dimensions that are too large to easily visualize in their raw form. For example, the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model produces embeddings with a dimension of 768. To plot these high-dimensional vectors in two-dimensional space for visualization, the documentation uses a technique called t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding). The tSNE function from the sklearn.manifold library is used with parameters including the number of components (set to 2 for 2D plotting), perplexity (set to 15 in the example), and a random state of 42 for reproducibility.
questions.question: True or False: The documentation uses t-SNE to reduce embedding dimensions for 2D visualization.

questions.lessonContent: The documentation provides a specific example showing how to use one of the listed models for data visualization. The model used in the visualization code example is the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model, which supports up to 8192 context length. The API string for this model is explicitly provided in the code as "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval". This model is passed to the sample_and_extract_embeddings function along with the context length parameter of 8192. The model allows generating embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings.
questions.question: What is the correct API string for the model used in the data visualization example?
questions.explanation: The documentation explicitly states that the model used for the data visualization example is "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval" with a context_length of 8192.

questions.lessonContent: The data visualization example in the Together Embeddings documentation demonstrates how to visualize sample data from RedPajama-v1 using embeddings. The process involves transforming high-dimensional embedding vectors (768 dimensions for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K) into a 2D representation that can be plotted. This requires first transforming the embedding vectors using tSNE, then plotting the transformed vectors with labels, and finally displaying the resulting visualization to see how texts from different data sources cluster together.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the data visualization workflow using Together Embeddings and tSNE?

questions.lessonTitle: Purpose of Continued Pretraining in Composer 2
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage aims to improve the language model's base knowledge, specifically in the domain of coding. This continued pretraining has long been demonstrated to drastically improve downstream performance. The purpose of this stage is to provide a base model for the subsequent agentic RL training by specializing the model on coding knowledge and capabilities. They extend Kimi K2.5 with a continued pretraining stage on a large code-dominated data mix.
questions.question: What is the purpose of the continued pretraining stage in Composer 2?
questions.answer: To provide a base model for the subsequent agentic RL training by specializing the model on coding knowledge and capabilities

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 was built using a selected base model chosen through internal evaluations measuring codebase perplexity, coding knowledge, and state tracking. After evaluating several potential open-source base models including GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and DeepSeek V3.2, the team selected Kimi K2.5 as the base model for Composer 2. Kimi K2.5 is a 1.04T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 32B active parameters.
questions.question: Composer 2 uses Kimi K2.5 as its base model.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage is divided into three phases. First, the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length. Second, there is a shorter long-context extension phase that extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. Third, there is a short supervised fine-tuning phase on targeted coding tasks. During training, the evaluation loss on the internal codebase decreases log-linearly over the course of the training run.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the three phases of continued pretraining in Composer 2?
choices: 16k token sequence length, then 256k long-context extension, then medium SFT on coding tasks
32k token sequence length, then 256k long-context extension, then short SFT on coding tasks
64k token sequence length, then 128k long-context extension, then long SFT on coding tasks
32k token sequence length, then 512k long-context extension, then long SFT on coding tasks
questions.explanation: The three phases are: 1) bulk of compute at 32k token sequence length, 2) shorter long-context extension phase to 256k sequence length, and 3) short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks.

questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 continued pretraining process involves extending a base model through multiple phases. First, we spend the bulk of compute at Phase 1: 32k Sequence Training, which focuses on the main training workload. Next, we conduct Phase 2: Long-Context Extension to extend the sequence length to 256k tokens. Finally, we complete with Phase 3: SFT on Coding Tasks, a short supervised fine-tuning phase on targeted coding tasks. This sequential approach progressively improves the model's coding knowledge and capabilities.
questions.question: What is the correct order of phases in the Composer 2 continued pretraining stage?

questions.lessonContent: To enable Composer 2 to work across long horizons, the model uses the self-summarization technique introduced in Composer 1.5. Each training rollout can involve multiple generations chained together by summaries, rather than a single prompt-response pair. The final reward is applied to all tokens produced by the model in the chain, upweighting both the agent responses in good trajectories and also the self-summarizations that made them work. Poor summaries that lose critical information are downweighted. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information, even with a limited context window. For hard examples, the model often self-summarizes multiple times.
questions.question: What specific technique does Composer 2 use to enable the model to work across long horizons?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a policy gradient algorithm with multiple samples per prompt and operates in the single-epoch regime. Following Dr. GRPO, they found it crucial to minimize bias in gradients that can arise from transforming the underlying advantage. They remove the length standardization term from GRPO as it introduces a length bias. Importantly, they do NOT normalize group advantages by their standard deviation, as this results in the degenerate case where small behavioral differences get massively upweighted within a group where every rollout achieves equal correctness.
questions.question: Composer 2 normalizes group advantages by their standard deviation during RL training.

questions.lessonContent: To incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests, Composer 2 adds a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to the reward. The formula is: Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)), where k and q are hyperparameters which define the curvature of the penalty. The input x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout. The nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks, achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks.
questions.question: Which formula does Composer 2 use for its nonlinear length penalty?
questions.explanation: The correct formula is Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)), which creates a concave down, increasing penalty that encourages quick solutions on easy tasks while allowing more thinking on hard tasks.

questions.lessonContent: In the Composer 2 reinforcement learning pipeline, the process begins by sampling a problem from our distribution, then simulating rollouts where the agent attempts different solutions, and finally evaluating these solutions to determine their quality. This sequential approach ensures the model learns from diverse problem-solving attempts.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 RL training loop when the agent first encounters a new problem?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite developed by Cursor to address limitations in public coding benchmarks. Unlike public benchmarks that are highly specified with narrow solution spaces, CursorBench features more under-specified prompts with a median description length of only 390 characters compared to 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. Additionally, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed versus just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. The benchmark is continuously evolved as user workflows change and agent capabilities improve, with CursorBench-3 more than doubling the median task size from earlier versions.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks compared to public benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services that enable large-scale global training with high availability and independent scaling. These services include training, environments, inference, and evaluations. The training service uses a fully asynchronous, high-throughput stack built on Ray and PyTorch, with a centralized reconciler managing sample lifecycle state through a pipeline of distributed executors. The environments service runs on Anyrun, an internal compute platform for running untrusted code at scale, where each pod is a dedicated Firecracker VM capable of running a full development environment including a browser and GUI for computer use.
questions.question: Is it true that Composer 2's RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services?

questions.lessonTitle: Precision Formats in MoE Training Kernels
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 training uses both MXFP8 and NVFP4 precision formats for the mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer, exclusively targeting NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs for block-scaled tensor-core matrix multiplications with in-hardware dequantization. For the MoE forward pass, a novel variant of NVFP4 is used where values are quantized from BF16 into FP4E2M1 using FP8E4M3 per-block scales with block size 16 and FP32 per-token scales. For the MoE backward pass, the standard MXFP8 format with FP8E4M3 values and FP8E8M0 scales per 32-element block is used. The asymmetry in RL training allows this because the forward pass must match inference for numerical stability while the backward pass runs only on the training cluster where higher precision improves training stability.
questions.question: Which precision format does Composer 2 use for the MoE forward pass to match inference numerical stability?
questions.explanation: The forward pass uses NVFP4 with per-token scaling to support fast inference and match numerical stability with the inference engine, while the backward pass uses MXFP8 for higher precision and training stability.

questions.lessonContent: The online evaluation process in Composer 2 involves several sequential steps to assess model performance. First, for each training step to evaluate, the system acquires a lease for an evaluation deployment and automatically moves GPUs to that deployment. Then, a cross-region weight sync is performed to transfer the evaluation checkpoint from the training cluster to the inference deployment. After the weights are synchronized, the evaluation runs using the production backend with the Cursor harness. Once the evaluation runs complete, accuracy metrics are computed to measure functional correctness. Finally, efficiency metrics like completion tokens, end-to-end latency, and inference cost are measured to ensure the model remains useful for interactive developer workflows.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 online evaluation pipeline?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, developer environment setup, and any unexpected behaviors or warnings particular to the project. You can place CLAUDE.md files in the root of your repo, any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of that directory, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: What is the name of the special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonTitle: Allowed Tools Management in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system: file writes, many bash commands, MCP tools, etc. We designed Claude Code with this deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Claude Code has a deliberately conservative approach to tool permissions, prioritizing safety over flexibility.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md files can be placed in several locations to control their context scope. The most common usage is placing CLAUDE.md in the root of your repo, or wherever you run claude from—you can name it CLAUDE.md and check it into git to share across sessions and with your team, or name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it. You can also place CLAUDE.md in any parent of the directory where you run claude, which is most useful for monorepos. Additionally, you can place CLAUDE.md in any child of the directory where you run claude, and Claude will pull in those files on demand when you work with files in those child directories. Finally, you can place CLAUDE.md in your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies it to all your claude sessions.
questions.question: In which of the following locations can CLAUDE.md files be placed for context?
choices: All of these locations (root, parent directory, child directory, home folder)
Only parent directories of where claude is run
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states CLAUDE.md files can be placed in the root of your repo, any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of that directory, or your home folder (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md).

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonTitle: Setting Up Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: When customizing your Claude Code environment, you first create CLAUDE.md files to document commands, code style guidelines, and workflow instructions. Once created, you then tune CLAUDE.md files by refining instructions, adding emphasis with keywords like IMPORTANT, and experimenting to determine what produces the best instruction following. After tuning, you add bash tools by telling Claude the tool name with usage examples and documenting frequently used tools in CLAUDE.md.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps when setting up and customizing your Claude Code environment?

questions.lessonTitle: The Explore, Plan, Code, Commit Workflow
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code doesn't impose a specific workflow, giving you the flexibility to use it how you want. One successful pattern is the explore, plan, code, commit workflow. First, ask Claude to read relevant files without writing code. Second, ask Claude to make a plan using the word 'think' to trigger extended thinking mode, which gives Claude additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly. The specific phrases mapped to increasing levels of thinking budget are: 'think' < 'think hard' < 'think harder' < 'ultrathink.' Each level allocates progressively more thinking budget. If the results seem reasonable, you can have Claude create a document or GitHub issue with its plan. Third, ask Claude to implement its solution in code. Fourth, ask Claude to commit the result and create a pull request. Steps #1-#2 are crucial—without them, Claude tends to jump straight to coding.
questions.question: What is the correct order of thinking budget phrases from lowest to highest?
questions.answer: think < think hard < think harder < ultrathink

questions.lessonTitle: Course Correction Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: While Claude Code can solve problems perfectly on the first attempt, using correction tools generally produces better solutions faster. There are four key tools for course correction. First, ask Claude to make a plan before coding and explicitly tell it not to code until you've confirmed its plan looks good. Second, press Escape to interrupt Claude during any phase—thinking, tool calls, or file edits—preserving context so you can redirect or expand instructions. Third, double-tap Escape to jump back in history, edit a previous prompt, and explore a different direction. Fourth, ask Claude to undo changes, often in conjunction with the second option to take a different approach. While auto-accept mode (shift+tab to toggle) lets Claude work autonomously, you'll typically get better results by being an active collaborator and guiding Claude's approach.
questions.question: Pressing Escape once interrupts Claude during any phase while preserving context.

questions.lessonTitle: Optimizing Data Input for Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Several methods exist for providing data to Claude Code during your workflow. The most common approach is to copy and paste directly into your prompt. You can also pipe data into Claude Code using command line syntax (e.g., cat foo.txt | claude), which is particularly useful for logs, CSVs, and large data files. Additionally, you can tell Claude to pull data via bash commands, MCP tools, or custom slash commands. Another option is to ask Claude to read files or fetch URLs, which works for images as well. Most sessions involve a combination of these approaches. For example, you can pipe in a log file, then tell Claude to use a tool to pull in additional context to debug the logs. When working with visual targets, you can paste screenshots, drag and drop images directly into the prompt input, or provide file paths for images.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most common method for passing data into Claude?
choices: Pipe into Claude Code using cat foo.txt | claude
Tell Claude to pull data via bash commands
Ask Claude to read files or fetch URLs
Copy and paste directly into your prompt
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states 'Copy and paste directly into your prompt (most common approach)' as the first method listed for passing data into Claude.

questions.lessonContent: The test-driven development workflow using Claude Code follows a specific sequence. First, you ask Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs. Second, you tell Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail—this is the crucial step where you explicitly instruct Claude not to write any implementation code. Third, you ask Claude to commit the tests when satisfied with them. Only after committing the failing tests does the actual implementation begin.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the test-driven development workflow using Claude Code?

questions.lessonTitle: Headless Mode Flag for Non-Interactive Execution
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag with a prompt. Additionally, the --output-format stream-json flag enables streaming JSON output. It's important to note that headless mode does not persist between sessions, meaning you have to trigger it each session rather than having it carry over.
questions.question: What flag is used to enable headless mode in Claude Code for non-interactive contexts?

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees Enable Parallel Claude Sessions
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. Using git worktrees enables you to run multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project, each focused on its own independent task. For example, you might have one Claude refactoring your authentication system while another builds a completely unrelated data visualization component. Since the tasks don't overlap, each Claude can work at full speed without waiting for the other's changes or dealing with merge conflicts.
questions.question: Git worktrees enable multiple Claude sessions to run simultaneously on different parts of a project with isolated working directories.

questions.lessonTitle: Fanning Out Pattern for Large-Scale Automation
questions.lessonContent: There are two primary patterns for using headless mode with a custom harness. Fanning out handles large migrations or analyses, such as analyzing sentiment in hundreds of logs or analyzing thousands of CSVs. The process involves having Claude write a script to generate a task list (for example, generating a list of 2k files that need to be migrated), then looping through tasks by calling Claude programmatically for each and giving it a specific task and set of tools. Pipelining integrates Claude into existing data processing pipelines by calling claude -p with your prompt and piping the JSON output to the next command in your processing pipeline.
questions.question: Which of the following headless mode patterns involves generating a task list and looping through tasks by calling Claude programmatically for each?
questions.explanation: Fanning out is the pattern that involves having Claude write a script to generate a task list, then looping through tasks by calling Claude programmatically for each task with a specific task and set of tools.

questions.lessonContent: The multiClaude workflow for code review and editing involves a sequential handoff process between different Claude instances. First, you use Claude to write code for your task. Then, you either run /clear or start a second Claude instance to review the first Claude's work. Finally, you have this second Claude provide feedback that can be used by a subsequent Claude to edit the code. This separation of writing, reviewing, and editing across different Claude instances often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything, as each instance maintains fresh context for its specific role.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multiClaude code review and editing workflow?

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images appear smooth and continuous but are actually composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numerical values representing the amount of red, green, and blue to mix together, with each value ranging from 0 (no color) to 255 (maximum intensity). A standard HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels, and since each pixel requires 3 bytes (one for each RGB channel), an uncompressed image would be approximately 6.2 megabytes. This raw data size demonstrates why compression is essential for practical image storage and transmission.
questions.question: How many numerical values (color channels) does each pixel contain in a standard RGB image?

questions.lessonTitle: The Two Fundamental Approaches to Compression
questions.lessonContent: There are two primary solutions for reducing image file sizes. The first approach involves throwing away data, which is called lossy compression and exploits how human vision works by removing details humans won't notice. The second approach involves being clever about how every pixel is stored, which is called lossless compression and preserves every single pixel while still achieving compression through clever encoding. These two fundamental ideas form the foundation for all major image formats including JPEG, PNG, ZIP files, and most web traffic. Lossy compression typically achieves 10-20x smaller files, while lossless compression achieves 3-50x reduction depending on the image content.
questions.question: It is possible to reduce an image file size without losing any pixel data by using clever encoding techniques.

questions.lessonContent: Image compression addresses the fundamental problem that raw image data requires significant storage space. An HD image containing 1920 × 1080 pixels requires approximately 6.2 megabytes to store all pixel values without any compression. To make images more manageable, compression methods work by either removing data that won't be perceived by humans or by finding more efficient ways to represent the same information. The lossless approach uses techniques like filtering (predicting pixel values from neighbors), pattern matching (finding repeated sequences), and encoding common values with shorter codes. The lossy approach exploits limitations in human visual perception to discard information that won't be noticed.
questions.question: What is the primary problem that image compression aims to solve?
choices: Improving image resolution for better quality
Large storage requirements for uncompressed image data
Enabling images to be printed in color
Making images display faster on screens
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that images like an HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels and requires 6.2 megabytes, and 'You need a way to shrink this to a more manageable size.' This clearly identifies the core problem as the large storage requirements of uncompressed images.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses lossless compression to preserve every pixel while shrinking file size. First, Apply Filtering stores differences between pixels rather than absolute values. Next, LZ77 Pattern Finding replaces repeated patterns with back-references. Finally, Huffman Encoding gives common values shorter binary codes.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonTitle: JPEG Block Processing in Image Compression
questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides an image into small squares before compression. Each image gets broken down into 8×8 pixel blocks. For each block, JPEG applies a mathematical transform that separates the data into different frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradient areas with gradual color changes, while high frequencies capture fine details like sharp edges and textures. Since photographs contain mostly smooth gradients, most of the important visual information ends up concentrated in just a few low-frequency components. This block-based approach allows JPEG to efficiently identify and remove visual details that are less noticeable to the human eye.
questions.question: In JPEG compression, into how many pixel blocks does the algorithm divide the image for processing?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonTitle: Human Vision and Color Resolution in JPEG
questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression takes advantage of specific limitations in human vision. The human eye is excellent at detecting brightness changes in fine detail but relatively poor at distinguishing small color differences. When colors blend together slightly, our vision blurs them rather than registering each distinct shade. JPEG exploits this by converting pixel data from RGB format into a representation that separates brightness from color information. The algorithm then reduces color resolution significantly because the human eye won't notice these slight color imperfections. Meanwhile, brightness details are preserved more carefully since we are highly sensitive to those variations.
questions.question: JPEG reduces color resolution while preserving brightness detail because the human eye is more sensitive to brightness changes than to color differences.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonContent: When JPEG processes each 8×8 block, it transforms the pixel data into frequency components using a mathematical technique. These frequency components represent different aspects of the visual information in the block. The low-frequency components contain information about smooth gradient areas and overall color trends in that block. The high-frequency components capture sharp edges, fine textures, and detailed patterns. Since typical photographs consist mainly of smooth gradient areas with gradual color transitions, most of the visually significant information resides in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG discards the high-frequency details that humans typically cannot perceive, resulting in much smaller file sizes while maintaining acceptable visual quality.
questions.question: Which type of frequency component does JPEG primarily keep in a compressed image?
questions.explanation: JPEG keeps low-frequency components because photographs mostly contain smooth gradient areas, and these components preserve the overall visual appearance while high-frequency details that are discarded are less noticeable to humans.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Human Vision
questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression exploits how human vision works. Our eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. To take advantage of this, JPEG first converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. It also reduces color resolution since our eyes won't notice. Then it divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the JPEG lossy compression pipeline?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG and Modern Algorithms
questions.lessonContent: PNG uses filtering or prediction to reduce file size by storing differences between adjacent pixels instead of their actual values. Instead of storing each value directly, PNG stores how much each pixel differs from its neighbor. PNG supports four prediction methods: Sub predicts from the left neighbor (best for horizontal gradients), Up predicts from the pixel above (best for vertical gradients), Average predicts from the average of left and above, and Paeth intelligently picks between left, above, or diagonal. PNG encoders try each method per row and pick the one that compresses best.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method is best suited for horizontal gradients?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG and Modern Algorithms
questions.lessonContent: After filtering, PNG uses an algorithm called LZ77 to find and replace repeated patterns with back-references. Instead of storing the same sequence twice, LZ77 says 'go back X values and copy Y' - this tiny reference is smaller than repeating the values. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data. Any pattern within that window can be referenced instead of repeated. For images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients, this significantly reduces file size.
questions.question: LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data, allowing any pattern within that window to be referenced instead of repeated.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG and Modern Algorithms
questions.lessonTitle: PNG Compression Ratios for Different Image Types
questions.lessonContent: PNG combines filtering, LZ77 pattern-finding, and Huffman coding to achieve lossless compression. For a photograph like a sunset, a 6.2 MB image becomes approximately 2.1 MB, achieving about 3x smaller file size with zero quality loss. Screenshots with large solid color regions can achieve much higher compression ratios, typically between 10x and 50x. The actual compression ratio depends heavily on the image content - images with more repeated patterns compress better.
questions.question: Which type of image typically achieves higher compression ratios in PNG: photographs or screenshots with large solid color regions?
choices: Screenshots with large solid color regions
questions.explanation: Screenshots with large solid color regions have more repeated patterns that LZ77 can reference and that Huffman coding can compress efficiently, achieving 10-50x compression compared to photographs which typically achieve only about 3x compression.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Octavian's Rise and Transformation into Augustus
questions.lessonContent: Octavian was sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. The Senate gave him the name Augustus, which means "most high." In 23 BCE, Octavian, now referred to as Augustus, was made consul for life by the Senate. He was also made "Princeps," meaning "first citizen," which is the origin of the word "prince." Additionally, he was made "Imperator," meaning "successful general," which is the origin of the word "emperor." He was also given the title "Pontifex Maximus," meaning "chief religious leader," which is the origin of the word "pontiff" used to describe the pope today.
questions.question: What title did the Senate give to Octavian that became the origin of the word "emperor"?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Concept of Primus Inter Pares
questions.lessonContent: Primus inter pares is a Latin phrase meaning "first among equals." Augustus and later emperors tried to maintain the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators. Being "first among equals" gave the illusion that an emperor was the most prestigious and important member of the Roman Senate, but that each senator was simultaneously equally important. In reality, the Roman emperors ruled with little input from anyone else.
questions.question: Roman emperors used the phrase primus inter pares to maintain the appearance of being elected officials rather than dictators. True or false?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Establishment of the Roman Empire
