questions.lessonContent: There was great variety in the quality of emperors who succeeded Augustus. The office of emperor was initially designed to be hereditary, but from the start, there was confusion as to which family member would inherit the throne. Some emperors proved to be cutthroats, or insane, or both. The military came to play an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor. Caligula, who ruled from 37-41 CE, earned his name "little boots" from the Roman army as a child because he was dressed like a soldier. After two years of good rule, he was followed by two years of horrible rule where he exiled, killed, or forced suicide upon members of his family and perceived enemies. Nero, who ruled from 54-68 CE, was considered a tyrant who murdered his mother, his stepbrother, and two of his wives, along with his teacher Seneca.
questions.question: Which Roman emperor was given his nickname "Caligula" (meaning "little boots") because he was dressed like a soldier as a child?
questions.explanation: Caligula earned his nickname "Caligula," meaning "little boots," from the Roman army as a child because he was dressed like a soldier. Caligula was the son of Germanicus and ruled from 37-41 CE.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate then gave him the name Augustus, meaning most high. Finally, in 23 BCE, Augustus was made consul for life by the Senate, which cemented his position as the first Roman emperor.
questions.question: What is the correct chronological order of the key steps in Octavian becoming Augustus and establishing the Roman Empire?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Height and Decline of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, meaning 'Roman Peace,' was a period when Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, establishing complete control that resulted in almost no warfare. This peace lasted nearly 200 years, from approximately 27 BCE to 180 CE. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship. The Pax Romana represented the height of Roman imperial power and stability, allowing for unprecedented economic and cultural exchange across the empire.
questions.question: What was the Pax Romana, and how long did this period of peace last?
questions.answer: The Pax Romana was a period of Roman peace and control of the Mediterranean region that lasted nearly 200 years.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Height and Decline of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: The office of emperor was initially designed to be hereditary, with power passing from one family member to another. However, from the start of the Empire, there was confusion as to which family member would inherit the throne. Some emperors proved to be cutthroats, or insane, or both. The military came to play an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor, often ignoring hereditary claims entirely.
questions.question: True or false: The office of Roman emperor was designed to be hereditary, but in practice the military played an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Height and Decline of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Claudius became emperor in 41 CE because he was the last adult male of his family. He was the brother of Germanicus and uncle of Caligula. When Caligula was assassinated by members of the Praetorian Guard in 41 CE, Claudius found himself as the last remaining adult male of the Julian family line. This made him the unexpected choice for emperor, as the military was seeking a candidate who could provide stability and legitimacy.
questions.question: Why did Claudius become emperor in 41 CE?
choices: The Roman Senate unanimously selected him
He was the last adult male of his family (brother of Germanicus and uncle of Caligula)
He voluntarily claimed the throne after Caligula's death
He was a famous military general who won the support of the army
questions.explanation: Claudius became emperor because he was the last adult male of his family - the brother of Germanicus and uncle of Caligula. With the assassination of Caligula, he was the sole surviving adult male of the Julian family line, making him the unexpected choice for the Praetorian Guard to elevate to the throne.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Height and Decline of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Decline and Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Following the period of instability during the Year of the Four Emperors, the Roman Empire faced increasing administrative challenges. Emperor Diocletian first divided the empire into eastern and western administrative realms in 285 CE, believing this would strengthen governance. Later, Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium (renamed Constantinople), further deepening the east-west division. Ultimately, the Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE when the last emperor Romulus Augustus was deposed by the barbarian Odoacer.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the administrative division and eventual fall of the Western Roman Empire?

questions.lessonTitle: Preservation and Transmission of Greek Culture by Rome
questions.lessonContent: The Romans played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting Greek (Hellenistic) culture to the West. While the Romans did not necessarily create everything they are credited for, they were particularly skilled at taking innovations like the Etruscan arch, adapting them, and putting them to great use. Greek texts and ideas were popular in Rome. When Rome fell, the Catholic Church, particularly monks, continued to preserve and transmit Greek texts and ideas to future generations. This transmission was vital for maintaining classical knowledge through the Middle Ages.
questions.question: What was the primary role the Romans played regarding Greek (Hellenistic) culture?
questions.answer: Preserving and transmitting it to the West

questions.lessonTitle: The Justinian Code and Roman Law
questions.lessonContent: Roman law started with the Twelve Tables in 450 BCE and developed over a thousand years, including decisions of judges, ideas of the Republic and Empire, and rulings of emperors. It encompassed public law (relationship of citizen to state), private or civil law (relationships between people), and peoples law (rights of foreigners). Emperor Justinian rewrote Roman law in the 6th century CE, creating the Corpus Juris Civilis, also known as the Justinian Code. This code encapsulated the previous thousand years of Roman law and still serves as the basis for civil law in several countries today.
questions.question: True or false: The Justinian Code was the first example of Roman law, developed in the early Republic period.

questions.lessonContent: The Romance languages developed from Latin and include French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish. English, in contrast, is a Germanic language. William the Conqueror brought French to England in 1066, and about half of modern English can be traced to Latin. The Catholic Church preserved Latin, and Catholic masses were said in Latin until the 1960s. Scientists have traditionally used Latin as a universal language, and our scientific names and most legal and medical terminology are derived from Latin.
questions.question: Which of the following is a Romance language that developed from Latin?
questions.explanation: French is a Romance language that developed from Latin. German is a Germanic language, not a Romance language. Italian and Spanish are also Romance languages that developed from Latin.

questions.lessonTitle: The Legacy of Rome: Roman Law
questions.lessonContent: Roman law began with the Twelve Tables, the first written code of laws in 450 BCE. Over the centuries, judges during the Republic added their decisions and interpretations to the legal system. When the Empire was established, additional rulings were incorporated. Individual emperors then contributed their own decisions and legal interpretations. Finally, in the 6th century CE, Emperor Justinian compiled and organized all these previous legal developments into the Justinian Code, which became the basis for civil law in many European countries.
questions.question: What is the correct chronological order of steps in the development of Roman law from its beginning to the Justinian Code?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, which are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish tasks. The Research feature uses an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. Each subagent operates with its own context window, exploring different aspects of a question in parallel before condensing the most important tokens for the lead research agent. This architecture provides separation of concerns through distinct tools, prompts, and exploration trajectories, which reduces path dependency and enables thorough, independent investigations.
questions.question: What is a multi-agent system according to the source content?
questions.answer: A system consisting of multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.lessonContent: Our Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information and then returning their findings to the lead agent so it can compile a final answer. Traditional approaches using Retrieval Augmented Generation use static retrieval, but our architecture uses multi-step search that dynamically finds relevant information.
questions.question: The Research system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates specialized subagents that operate in parallel.

questions.lessonTitle: Performance Gains from Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Our internal evaluations show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. We found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval. For example, when asked to identify all the board members of the companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found the correct answers by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single agent system failed to find the answer with slow, sequential searches. In our analysis, token usage alone explains 80% of performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation.
questions.question: By what percentage did the multi-agent system (with Claude Opus 4 as lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents) outperform single-agent Claude Opus 4 on the internal research evaluation?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states: 'We found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval.'

questions.lessonTitle: Small-Scale Testing in Early Agent Development
questions.lessonContent: In early agent development, changes tend to have dramatic impacts because there is abundant low-hanging fruit. A prompt tweak might boost success rates from 30% to 80%. With effect sizes this large, you can spot changes with just a few test cases. Anthropic started with a set of about 20 queries representing real usage patterns. Testing these queries often allowed them to clearly see the impact of changes. They often heard that AI developer teams delay creating evals because they believe that only large evals with hundreds of test cases are useful. However, it is best to start with small-scale testing right away with a few examples, rather than delaying until you can build more thorough evals.
questions.question: What approximate number of queries did Anthropic start with for early agent testing?

questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. LLMs are a natural fit for grading outputs. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (do claims match sources?), citation accuracy (do the cited sources match the claims?), completeness (are all requested aspects covered?), source quality (did it use primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources?), and tool efficiency (did it use the right tools a reasonable number of times?). They experimented with multiple judges to evaluate each component, but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.
questions.question: True or False: Anthropic found that using multiple LLM judges to evaluate each component of research outputs was more consistent than using a single LLM call with one prompt.

questions.lessonTitle: Prompt Engineering Principles for Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic documented eight principles for prompting research agents. These include: thinking like your agents by building simulations to understand their effects; teaching the orchestrator how to delegate by providing detailed task descriptions; scaling effort to query complexity with explicit resource allocation guidelines; making tool design and selection critical with explicit heuristics for tool use; letting agents improve themselves by using Claude models as prompt engineers; starting wide then narrowing search strategy; guiding the thinking process with extended thinking mode; and using parallel tool calling for speed and performance. These principles help instil good heuristics rather than rigid rules for agent behavior.
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the eight prompt engineering principles mentioned in the source content?
choices: Maximize token usage for all tasks
questions.explanation: The source explicitly mentions 'Scale effort to query complexity' as one of the eight principles - agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so scaling rules were embedded in the prompts to allocate resources efficiently.

questions.lessonTitle: Error Handling in Long-Running Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls. This means errors can compound and minor system failures can become catastrophic for agents. When errors occur, restarting from the beginning is expensive and frustrating for users. Anthropic built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred, rather than starting over. They also combine the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: How does Anthropic handle agent errors to avoid restarting from the beginning?
questions.answer: They built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred, combined with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.

questions.lessonContent: Agents make dynamic decisions and are non-deterministic between runs, even with identical prompts. This makes debugging harder because users would report agents not finding obvious information, but it was difficult to determine whether agents were using bad search queries, choosing poor sources, or hitting tool failures. Anthropic added full production tracing to diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically. They also monitor agent decision patterns and interaction structures without monitoring individual conversation contents to maintain user privacy.
questions.question: True or False: Because agents are non-deterministic between runs, debugging requires full production tracing to diagnose why agents failed.

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. When deploying updates, agents might be anywhere in their process, so well-meaning code changes could break existing agents. Anthropic cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, they use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: Which deployment strategy does Anthropic use to update agent systems without disrupting running agents?
choices: Rolling updates that restart agents one at a time in sequential order
Rainbow deployments that gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running
Blue-green deployments that run two completely separate environments
Immediate updates that replace all agents with the new version simultaneously
questions.explanation: Rainbow deployments gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously, preventing disruption to agents that might be anywhere in their process during updates.

questions.lessonContent: The debugging process for multi-agent systems follows a systematic approach. It begins by adding full production tracing to diagnose why agents fail, then involves monitoring agent decision patterns to observe behaviors, and continues with analyzing interaction structures to understand how agents coordinate. This high-level observability helps identify root causes and fix issues systematically.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the debugging process for multi-agent research systems?

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonTitle: Image Pixel Structure and Data Requirements
questions.lessonContent: Images appear smooth and continuous but are actually made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together, with each value ranging from 0 (none) to 255 (maximum). A standard HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels, and since each pixel needs 3 bytes (one for R, G, and B), the uncompressed file size is approximately 6.2 megabytes. This large file size demonstrates why compression is essential for storing and transmitting images efficiently.
questions.question: How many numbers does each pixel contain, and what is the range of each value?
questions.answer: Each pixel contains 3 numbers (RGB), and each value ranges from 0 to 255

questions.lessonContent: When you need every pixel to be perfect, such as screenshots with text or graphics with sharp edges, lossless compression is the solution. Lossless compression (used by PNG) preserves every single pixel while still reducing file size. It achieves this through three main techniques: predicting values from neighboring pixels, finding repeated patterns to reference instead of storing repeatedly, and using shorter binary codes for more common values. These techniques allow PNG to achieve 3x compression for photographs and 10-50x compression for screenshots with large solid color regions.
questions.question: Lossless compression can achieve perfect reconstruction of the original pixel data.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses a technique called filtering or prediction to reduce file size by storing how much each pixel differs from its neighbor rather than storing each value directly. The differences between adjacent pixels are usually small numbers, which are easier to compress than large values. PNG supports four prediction methods: Sub (predicts from the left neighbor, best for horizontal gradients), Up (predicts from the pixel above, best for vertical gradients), Average (predicts from the average of left and above), and Paeth (intelligently picks between left, above, or diagonal). PNG encoders try each method per row and select the one that achieves the best compression.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method is best for horizontal gradients?
choices: Average (predict from left and above average)
questions.explanation: The Sub method predicts from the left neighbor and is specifically noted as best for horizontal gradients in the source content.

questions.lessonContent: PNG lossless compression uses three main techniques to shrink image files while preserving every pixel. First, filtering predicts each pixel from its neighbors and stores only the differences. Then, LZ77 pattern finding replaces repeated sequences with compact references. Finally, Huffman encoding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently. This sequence of filtering, then LZ77, then Huffman enables PNG to achieve significant compression without losing any image data. The process wraps the final encoded data in the PNG file format to produce the compressed output.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in PNG lossless compression?

questions.lessonContent: JPEG begins by converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. This separation allows JPEG to treat brightness and color information differently during compression. Since human eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together, JPEG reduces color resolution while preserving brightness detail. This color space transformation is a crucial first step that enables the rest of the compression process to work effectively.
questions.question: To what format does JPEG convert pixels from RGB?
questions.answer: A format that separates brightness from color

questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Photographs are mostly smooth gradients, which means most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details that human eyes won't notice, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: JPEG keeps the high-frequency details in the compressed image and discards low-frequency components.

questions.lessonContent: When compressing an image, JPEG first divides the image into blocks before transforming them into frequency components. Each block is square and consists of a specific number of pixels that allows the mathematical transformation to work efficiently. The size of these blocks determines the granularity at which compression is applied and affects the appearance of artifacts at high compression levels.
questions.question: What is the size of the pixel blocks that JPEG uses for transformation?
questions.explanation: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components for compression.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression exploits how human vision works. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. The process begins by converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color, then reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice. After this, JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in JPEG color processing?

questions.lessonContent: LZ77 is a pattern-finding algorithm used in lossless compression that replaces repeated sequences with compact back-references. It maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data, and any pattern within that window can be referenced instead of being repeated. For example, instead of storing the same sequence twice like "0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2", LZ77 can say "go back 5 values and copy 5". This tiny reference is much smaller than repeating the values. For images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients, this significantly helps reduce file size.
questions.question: What is the size of the sliding window that LZ77 uses for pattern matching?

questions.lessonContent: After filtering and pattern-finding, some values appear more frequently than others in the compressed data. The value 0 (representing no difference between predicted and actual pixel values) might appear 60% of the time, while 127 might appear only 5%. Huffman coding gives common values shorter binary codes: 0 gets just 1 bit, 2 gets 2 bits, 255 gets 3 bits, and 127 gets 3 bits. Without Huffman coding, every value uses 8 bits. The math works out to be 5x smaller: 60×1 + 25×2 + 10×3 + 5×3 = 155 bits instead of 100×8 = 800 bits.
questions.question: In Huffman coding for PNG compression, does the algorithm assign shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently in the data?

questions.lessonTitle: PNG Compression Ratio for Different Image Types
questions.lessonContent: PNG lossless compression achieves different compression ratios depending on the type of image. For photographs like a sunset, a 6.2 MB image becomes around 2.1 MB, which is approximately 3x smaller with zero quality loss. However, screenshots with large solid color regions can achieve much higher compression ratios of 10-50x. This is because solid color regions have many identical adjacent pixels that the compression algorithms can efficiently predict and reference, whereas photographs have more varied pixel values that are harder to compress.
questions.question: Which type of image achieves higher compression ratios with PNG lossless compression: photographs or screenshots with large solid color regions?
choices: Screenshots with large solid color regions
questions.explanation: Screenshots with large solid color regions achieve 10-50x compression because identical adjacent pixels can be efficiently predicted and referenced, whereas photographs have more varied pixel values that are harder to compress.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Octavian was sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. The Senate gave him the name "Augustus," meaning "most high." In 23 BCE, Octavian, now referred to as Augustus, was made consul for life by the Senate. He was also made "Princeps," meaning "first citizen" (origin of the word "prince"), and "Imperator," meaning "successful general" (origin of the word "emperor"). He additionally held the title "Pontifex Maximus," meaning chief religious leader, which is the origin of the word "pontiff" used to describe the pope today.
questions.question: What does the name "Augustus" mean?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Duration of the Pax Romana
questions.lessonContent: Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, establishing complete control that meant almost no warfare. This period of peace was known as the Pax Romana, or Roman Peace. According to the source, this peace lasted nearly 200 years. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship.
questions.question: The Pax Romana lasted for approximately 200 years.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Augustus and the Concept of Primus Inter Pares
questions.lessonContent: "Primus inter pares" is a Latin phrase meaning "first among equals." Augustus and later emperors tried to maintain the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators. Being "first among equals" gave the illusion that an emperor was the most prestigious and important member of the Roman Senate, but that each senator was simultaneously equally important. In reality, the Roman emperors ruled with little input from anyone else.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the meaning of "primus inter pares"?
questions.explanation: "Primus inter pares" literally translates to "first among equals," reflecting the Roman emperors' attempt to appear as equal senators rather than absolute rulers, while still holding supreme power.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Peak and Decline of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen Rome. In 285 CE, he divided the empire into two administrative realms: the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire and the Western (Roman) Empire. This was the first step in creating what would become two separate empires. Once Constantine later set up Constantinople as a capital city, the east-west split deepened significantly.
questions.question: In what year did Diocletian divide the empire into Eastern and Western administrative realms?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Peak and Decline of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Vespasian ruled as Roman emperor from 69 to 79 CE. He is famous for building the Colosseum in Rome, which served as a place where gladiatorial combats were held. The construction of this massive amphitheater was one of his most notable achievements and remains an iconic symbol of ancient Rome today.
questions.question: Vespasian built the Colosseum in Rome for gladiatorial combats.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Peak and Decline of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Marcus Aurelius ruled from 161 to 180 CE and was a Stoic philosopher. He wrote the famous philosophical work called Meditations. He was succeeded by his son Commodus, who ruled from 180 to 192 CE. The end of Marcus Aurelius's reign marked the conclusion of the Pax Romana, which had lasted from 27 BCE to 180 CE. The characters in the Russell Crowe film Gladiator are very loosely based on Marcus Aurelius and his son Commodus.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes Marcus Aurelius?
choices: Ruler who divided the empire into east and west
questions.explanation: Marcus Aurelius was a Stoic philosopher who wrote the book Meditations during his reign as emperor from 161 to 180 CE.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event marks the traditional date used by historians to signify the end of ancient Rome's western half. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire, however, continued to exist for nearly another thousand years until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. This makes the fall of the Western Empire much earlier than the fall of the Eastern Empire by almost a millennium. The division between East and West began when Emperor Diocletian split the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE, a decision he believed would strengthen administration.
questions.question: In what year was the Western Roman Empire officially ended?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Constantine had a significant relationship with Christianity. His mother Helena had converted to Christianity before him. In 313 CE, Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, which legalized Christianity and established religious toleration throughout the empire. Constantine ultimately converted to Christianity on his deathbed. His support for Christianity was transformative for the religion, as future Roman emperors were also Christians. When the Western Roman Empire eventually fell apart, the city of Rome became the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church.
questions.question: Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, which made Christianity the official state religion of Rome.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Justinian was a powerful ruler of the Eastern (Byzantine) empire who managed to reunite the Eastern and Western empires for a time, though this reunification did not last. One of his most significant accomplishments was rewriting Roman law into what is known as the Corpus Juris Civilis, or the Justinian Code. This legal code encapsulated over a thousand years of Roman legal development and remains the basis for civil law in several countries today. Justinian also married Theodora, an intelligent courtesan who became his co-ruler.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes an accomplishment of Emperor Justinian?
choices: He established the Edict of Milan granting religious toleration
He moved the capital from Rome to Constantinople
He codified Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis, which influenced modern civil law
He built the Colosseum in Rome for gladiatorial combats
questions.explanation: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis (or Justinian Code) encapsulated over 1,000 years of Roman law and still forms the basis for civil law in several countries. The other options describe achievements of different emperors: Constantine moved the capital and issued the Edict of Milan, while Vespasian built the Colosseum.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Lasting Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: Economic Decline of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The economic decline of the Western Roman Empire followed a specific sequence of events. First, the wealth gap grows between the rich patricians and the poor commoners. Second, as poverty increases, the poor become coloni, tied to the land as agricultural workers. Third, with more people becoming dependent laborers, the lower class loses purchasing power for manufactured goods.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the economic decline of the Western Roman Empire?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern. In this architecture, a lead agent coordinates the entire research process while delegating specific tasks to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. Each subagent independently performs web searches, evaluates tool results using interleaved thinking, and returns findings to the lead agent. The lead agent then synthesizes these results and decides whether more research is needed before passing all findings to a CitationAgent for processing.
questions.question: What multi-agent architecture pattern does Anthropic's Research system use?

questions.lessonContent: The lead agent in Anthropic's Research system executes subagents synchronously. This means the lead agent waits for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding with the next step in the research process. Synchronous execution simplifies coordination between agents but creates bottlenecks in information flow. For instance, the lead agent cannot steer subagents in real-time, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. The system currently does not use asynchronous execution, though the engineers note that it would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed.
questions.question: The lead agent in Anthropic's Research system executes subagents asynchronously, allowing them to work concurrently without waiting for previous subagents to complete.

questions.lessonContent: In the BrowseComp evaluation, which tests the ability of browsing agents to locate hard-to-find information, Anthropic identified three factors that explain 95% of the performance variance. Token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, making it the dominant factor. The remaining explanatory factors are the number of tool calls and the model choice. This finding validates their multi-agent architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. The research shows that multi-agent systems effectively scale token usage for tasks that exceed the limits of single agents, as more tokens enable more thorough exploration of complex topics.
questions.question: According to the source content, what percentage of performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation is explained by token usage alone?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance in the BrowseComp evaluation, with the remaining factors (tool calls and model choice) accounting for the other 15%.

questions.lessonContent: When teaching the orchestrator how to delegate, each subagent needs specific components to execute tasks effectively. Each subagent requires an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information. Anthropic found that simple, short instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage' were often vague enough that subagents misinterpreted the task or performed the exact same searches as other agents.
questions.question: According to the source content, what four components must each subagent receive from the lead agent to execute tasks effectively?
questions.answer: An objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic discovered that Claude 4 models can be excellent prompt engineers when given a prompt and a failure mode. These models can diagnose why an agent is failing and suggest improvements. They even created a tool-testing agent that, when given a flawed MCP tool, attempts to use the tool and then rewrites the tool description to avoid failures. By testing the tool dozens of times, this agent found key nuances and bugs.
questions.question: Claude 4 models can act as prompt engineers to improve agent behavior when given a prompt and a failure mode.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Effort Guidelines for Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: Agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so scaling rules must be embedded in prompts. For simple fact-finding tasks, only 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls is needed. Direct comparisons might require 2-4 subagents with 10-15 tool calls each. Complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries.
questions.question: According to Anthropic's scaling guidelines, how many subagents and tool calls are recommended for simple fact-finding versus direct comparison queries?
choices: Simple fact-finding: 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls; Direct comparisons: 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each
Simple fact-finding: 2-3 agents with 15-20 tool calls; Direct comparisons: 5-7 subagents with 25-30 calls each
Simple fact-finding: 3-5 agents with 5-10 tool calls; Direct comparisons: 4-6 subagents with 15-20 calls each
Simple fact-finding: 1-2 agents with 10-15 tool calls; Direct comparisons: 2-3 subagents with 20-30 calls each
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, while direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each. These specific numbers are part of the scaling rules embedded in prompts to help agents allocate resources efficiently.

questions.lessonContent: Effective evaluation of multi-agent research systems requires a sequential approach. First, you should start evaluating immediately with small samples, using about 20 queries representing real usage patterns to spot dramatic impacts from early changes. Second, you should use LLM-as-judge evaluation which scales well for grading research outputs against criteria like factual accuracy, citation accuracy, and completeness. Third, you should apply human evaluation to catch edge cases that automated evals miss, such as hallucinated answers on unusual queries or subtle source selection biases. This progression from small-sample testing through automated LLM judging to human verification forms the core evaluation workflow.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent research system evaluation workflow?

questions.lessonTitle: Error Recovery Strategies for Stateful Agents
questions.lessonContent: Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls, which means errors can compound quickly. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents. When errors occur, restarting from the beginning is expensive and frustrating for users. Anthropic built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred. They also leverage the model's intelligence to handle issues gracefully by letting the agent know when a tool is failing and allowing it to adapt. This combines the adaptability of AI agents with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: What approach does Anthropic use to handle errors in long-running agent systems instead of restarting from the beginning?
questions.answer: They built systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred, combining AI adaptability with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and checkpoints.

questions.lessonTitle: Deployment Strategy for Stateful Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means whenever Anthropic deploys updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. They need to prevent well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. Updating every agent to the new version simultaneously is not feasible. Instead, they use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: Rainbow deployments gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously to avoid disrupting running agents.

questions.lessonContent: Agents make dynamic decisions and are non-deterministic between runs, even with identical prompts, making debugging harder. Users would report agents not finding obvious information, but developers couldn't see why. Were agents using bad search queries, choosing poor sources, or hitting tool failures? Adding full production tracing let Anthropic diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically. Beyond standard observability, they monitor agent decision patterns and interaction structures without monitoring individual conversation contents to maintain user privacy. This high-level observability helped diagnose root causes, discover unexpected behaviors, and fix common failures.
questions.question: What specific aspect of agent behavior does Anthropic monitor for debugging without monitoring individual conversation contents?
choices: Agent decision patterns and interaction structures
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states they monitor 'agent decision patterns and interaction structures' without monitoring the contents of individual conversations to maintain user privacy.

questions.lessonContent: The multi-agent research system follows a structured workflow where the lead agent coordinates specialized subagents to explore complex topics. The process begins with user input, where a LeadResearcher agent analyzes the query and develops a research strategy. It then creates specialized subagents with specific research tasks, each performing independent web searches and returning findings. The lead agent synthesizes these results and determines if additional research is needed before passing findings to a CitationAgent for proper attribution.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent research system workflow?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Together Embeddings and Available Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released with 8 open source embedding models. These include top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, along with the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context which come in three variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths. The platform offers these models at competitive prices, being up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.
questions.question: How many embedding models are available through the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Together Embeddings and Available Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers models that achieve state-of-the-art performance in MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark). These models show comparable or even better accuracies than closed models from companies like OpenAI and Cohere. Specifically, the available models outperform OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3 in both MTEB and LoCo Benchmarks. This performance is achieved while maintaining significantly lower costs compared to other platforms.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint includes models that achieve state-of-the-art performance in MTEB.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Together Embeddings and Available Models
questions.lessonContent: The M2-BERT retrieval models are specifically designed for long context tasks and come in three variants. The 2k model supports up to 2,000 tokens in context, the 8k model supports up to 8,000 tokens, and the 32k model supports up to 32,000 tokens. These models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks, allowing users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks.
questions.question: Which of the following is a context length variant available for M2-BERT retrieval models?
questions.explanation: M2-BERT retrieval models are available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens. The 32k variant supports up to 32,000 tokens, making it the correct answer among the choices provided.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint is designed with full OpenAI compatibility, meaning developers who have already built applications using the OpenAI API can easily switch to the Together endpoint. To migrate, you simply need to update your API configuration by specifying the Together API key and setting the base URL to 'https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings'. The client initialization uses the OpenAI library but with these modified parameters. This compatibility allows existing code to work with minimal changes, making the transition seamless for teams already familiar with the OpenAI embeddings interface.
questions.question: What two parameters must be configured to make the OpenAI client work with the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides integrations with popular frameworks and databases for building Retrieval Augmented Generation systems. According to the content, the platform supports integration with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for RAG applications. These integrations allow developers to combine embeddings generation with vector storage and retrieval capabilities. The documentation provides specific tutorials for building RAG using Together with each of these platforms, enabling developers to choose the tools that best fit their existing workflows.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint supports integrations with Pinecone, Chroma, MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for building RAG systems.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers significant cost advantages compared to other popular embedding platforms. The pricing structure allows developers to access the embedding models at rates that are up to 4 times cheaper than competing services. This cost reduction applies across all 8 available embedding models, including the state-of-the-art M2-BERT retrieval models and the top-performing models from the MTEB leaderboard. The combination of lower cost with high performance makes it an attractive option for applications requiring large-scale embedding generation.
questions.question: Compared to other popular platforms, how much cheaper is the Together Embeddings endpoint?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that you can access these powerful models at very competitive prices, up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Data Visualization Applications
questions.lessonContent: The embedding dimension is a critical parameter when working with vector embeddings, as it determines the size of the numerical vector that represents each text. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model, which uses the API string togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval, the embedding dimension is 768. This dimension is typically too large to easily visualize in its raw form, which is why dimensionality reduction techniques become necessary for visualization purposes.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Data Visualization Applications
questions.lessonTitle: tSNE for Dimensionality Reduction in Visualization
questions.lessonContent: When working with high-dimensional embeddings, visualization requires reducing the dimensionality to make the data plotable in 2D or 3D space. The content demonstrates using tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) specifically for this purpose. The transform_tSNE function shown takes an embedding matrix and transforms it into a lower-dimensional representation suitable for plotting.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings data visualization example uses tSNE to transform embedding vectors into a lower-dimensional representation suitable for plotting.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Data Visualization Applications
questions.lessonContent: The data visualization example in the content demonstrates how to visualize sample data from the RedPajama-v1 dataset using embeddings. The code processes multiple data files representing different domains of text sources. In the main script, five specific data files are used: arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, github_sample.jsonl, and stackexchange_sample.jsonl. Each of these represents a different source domain, and the visualization shows how texts from each source cluster together based on their semantic similarity.
questions.question: Which of the following data sources is used in the RedPajama-v1 data visualization example?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is arxiv_sample.jsonl, which is explicitly listed in the main script alongside book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, github_sample.jsonl, and stackexchange_sample.jsonl.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundations - Model Architecture and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 model was built using Kimi K2.5 as its base model. Kimi K2.5 is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 1.04 trillion total parameters and 32 billion active parameters. This base model was selected after internal evaluations measuring codebase perplexity, coding knowledge through FreshBench, and state tracking capabilities. The selection process also considered inference performance considerations and general strong performance across multiple benchmarks.
questions.question: What is the name and parameter count of the base model used for Composer 2?
questions.answer: Kimi K2.5 with 1.04 trillion total parameters and 32 billion active parameters

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundations - Model Architecture and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is divided into three distinct phases. First, the bulk of compute is spent at a 32k token sequence length. Second, there is a shorter long-context extension phase that extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. Third, there is a short supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase focused on targeted coding tasks. During training, the evaluation loss on the internal codebase decreases log-linearly over the course of the training run.
questions.question: True or False: The continued pretraining stage consists of exactly three phases with sequence lengths of 32k, then 256k, followed by SFT.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundations - Model Architecture and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: To serve the model faster in production, Composer 2 trains additional Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers for use with speculative decoding. These MTP layers are initialized from scratch and trained on the same data mix as the main model. To speed up convergence, the MTP layers are trained with self-distillation, which teaches the model to predict the exact logit distribution of the main LM head at each position. The MTP layers are trained atop a checkpoint cut from the middle of the continued pretraining run, and during the final two phases (long-context and SFT), they are included and trained jointly with the rest of the model.
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of training Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers in Composer 2?
choices: Speculative decoding to serve the model faster in production
Enabling longer context lengths beyond 256k tokens
Reducing the number of RL training steps needed
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states 'To serve the model faster in production, we train additional Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers to use with speculative decoding.' This is the stated purpose of the MTP layers.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Module 2 - Reinforcement Learning for Code Generation
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses reinforcement learning trained on a large set of coding tasks in environments that emulate real Cursor sessions. The RL pipeline operates in a highly asynchronous regime with independent training and rollout generation workers. They use a policy gradient algorithm with multiple samples per prompt and a fixed group size, operating in the single-epoch regime where the same prompt is never trained on twice. Adam is used as the underlying optimizer and they update the full parameter set.
questions.question: What type of algorithm does Composer 2 use for reinforcement learning training?
questions.answer: Policy gradient algorithm with multiple samples per prompt

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Module 2 - Reinforcement Learning for Code Generation
questions.lessonContent: In the reinforcement learning training, Composer 2 found it crucial to minimize the bias in gradients that can arise from transforming the underlying advantage. Following Dr. GRPO work, they remove the length standardization term from GRPO as it introduces a length bias. Additionally, they do not normalize group advantages by their standard deviation, as this results in a degenerate case where small behavioral differences get massively upweighted within a group where every rollout achieves equal correctness.
questions.question: True or False: Composer 2 normalizes group advantages by their standard deviation in RL training.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Module 2 - Reinforcement Learning for Code Generation
questions.lessonContent: To incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests, Composer 2 adds a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to the reward. The formula is: Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)), where k and q are hyperparameters which define the curvature of the penalty, and the input x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout. The nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks.
questions.question: What is the formula for the nonlinear length penalty used to reward efficient coding behavior?
questions.explanation: The correct formula is Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)), where k and q are hyperparameters defining curvature, and x is a weighted combination of various token types and rollout metrics.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Module 3 - Evaluation Benchmarks, Infrastructure, and Results
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench, which is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. This represents a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 (which scored 44.2%) and a 61% improvement over Composer 1 (which scored 38.0%). The benchmark was specifically designed to address limitations in public evaluation sets, including domain mismatch, prompt over-specification, data contamination, and narrow evaluation scope.
questions.question: What is Composer 2's accuracy score on CursorBench?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Module 3 - Evaluation Benchmarks, Infrastructure, and Results
questions.lessonContent: CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications compared to public benchmarks, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. At the same time, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: True or False: CursorBench tasks require fewer lines of code changes than public benchmarks like SWE-bench.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Module 3 - Evaluation Benchmarks, Infrastructure, and Results
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 was also evaluated on two public benchmarks: SWE-bench Multilingual and Terminal-Bench. On SWE-bench Multilingual, Composer 2 scores 73.7%, which is a 7.8% improvement over Composer 1.5 (65.9%) and 16.8% over Composer 1 (56.9%). On Terminal-Bench, Composer 2 achieves 61.7%, improving upon Composer 1.5 by 13.8% and Composer 1 by 21.7%. These scores demonstrate performance competitive with state-of-the-art frontier models.
questions.question: What are the three benchmarks mentioned in the evaluation results table for Composer 2?
questions.explanation: The evaluation results table explicitly shows three benchmarks: CursorBench (61.3%), SWE-bench Multilingual (73.7%), and Terminal-Bench (61.7%) as the three columns in Table 1.

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo (where you run claude), which is the most common usage and can be checked into git; any parent of the directory where you run claude, useful for monorepos; any child of the directory where you run claude; and your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to apply it to all sessions. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: Where should you place a CLAUDE.md file if you want to check it into git and share it with your team?
questions.answer: The root of your repo (or wherever you run claude from)

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code supports placing CLAUDE.md files in your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies the configuration to all your Claude sessions. This allows you to have consistent instructions and documentation available regardless of which directory or project you are working in. The home folder location is one of several places Claude checks for context files, alongside the current working directory and its parent directories.
questions.question: CLAUDE.md files placed in the home folder (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) apply to all Claude Code sessions.

questions.lessonTitle: Managing Allowed Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, designed with a deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: selecting "Always allow" when prompted during a session, using the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools, manually editing your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, and using the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a way to manage allowed tools in Claude Code?
choices: Select "Always allow" when prompted during a session
Use the /permissions command to add or remove tools
Restart the Claude Code application to reset permissions
Use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'Restart the Claude Code application to reset permissions' because restarting is not mentioned as a method. The four documented ways are: selecting "Always allow" when prompted, using the /permissions command, manually editing settings.json, and using the --allowedTools CLI flag.

questions.lessonContent: When setting up Claude Code, the first step involves creating CLAUDE.md files in strategic locations such as the repository root, parent directories, or home folder. After creating these files, the next step is to tune your CLAUDE.md files by refining their content like any frequently used prompt, experimenting to determine what produces the best instruction following from the model. Once your CLAUDE.md files are tuned, you should then curate Claude's list of allowed tools to customize which tools Claude can use without prompting for permission.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in customizing your Claude Code setup?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code supports a versatile workflow pattern called Explore, Plan, Code, Commit. In the first step, you ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs while explicitly telling it not to write any code yet. The second step involves asking Claude to make a plan using the word 'think' to trigger extended thinking mode, which gives Claude additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly. These specific phrases map directly to increasing levels of thinking budget: 'think' is less than 'think hard', which is less than 'think harder', which is less than 'ultrathink'. Each level allocates progressively more thinking budget for Claude to use. Steps #1-#2 are crucial because without them, Claude tends to jump straight to coding a solution.
questions.question: In the Explore, Plan, Code, Commit workflow, which word should you use to trigger extended thinking mode for evaluating alternatives more thoroughly?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code excels at test-driven development (TDD) workflows. In this pattern, you first ask Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs and explicitly state that you're doing TDD so it avoids creating mock implementations. Next, you tell Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail, explicitly instructing it not to write any implementation code at this stage. Then you ask Claude to commit the tests when satisfied. Finally, you ask Claude to write code that passes the tests while instructing it not to modify the tests. Claude performs best when it has a clear target to iterate against, such as test cases, where it can make changes, evaluate results, and incrementally improve until it succeeds.
questions.question: In the TDD workflow with Claude Code, after writing tests and confirming they fail, should you explicitly tell Claude not to write any implementation code at this stage before it writes implementation code?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code provides multiple methods for receiving images to support visual development workflows. You can paste screenshots directly into the prompt input, with a pro tip being that on macOS you can hit cmd+ctrl+shift+4 to screenshot to clipboard and ctrl+v to paste (note this is not the standard cmd+v used for normal pasting and does not work remotely). Claude also accepts images via drag and drop directly into the prompt input, and you can provide file paths for images. These capabilities are particularly useful when working with design mocks as reference points for UI development, and visual charts for analysis and debugging.
questions.question: How many distinct methods does Claude Code provide for receiving images?
choices: Three: paste screenshots, drag and drop, and file paths
Two: paste and drag and drop only
Four: paste, drag and drop, file paths, and URLs
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states three methods: pasting screenshots, dragging and dropping images directly into the prompt input, and providing file paths for images.

questions.lessonContent: The 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow is one of the most versatile patterns for using Claude Code effectively. First, you should ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs to gather context about your codebase. Next, you ask Claude to make a plan for how to approach the specific problem, using words like 'think' to trigger extended thinking mode. After confirming the plan is reasonable, you ask Claude to implement the solution in code. Finally, you ask Claude to commit the result and create a pull request. This sequential approach prevents Claude from jumping straight to coding without proper research and planning.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow pattern?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Agent Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. Use the -p flag with a prompt to enable headless mode, and --output-format stream-json for streaming JSON output. Note that headless mode does not persist between sessions - you have to trigger it each time.
questions.question: What flag do you use to enable headless mode in Claude Code?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Agent Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Headless mode can power automations triggered by GitHub events, such as when a new issue is created in your repository. For example, the public Claude Code repository uses Claude to inspect new issues as they come in and assign appropriate labels. This allows automated handling of incoming issues without manual intervention.
questions.question: True or False: Headless mode can be used to automatically triage new GitHub issues as they are created.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Agent Workflows
questions.lessonContent: A simple but effective multi-Agent approach is to have one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it. Similar to working with multiple engineers, sometimes having separate context is beneficial. The workflow involves: use Claude to write code, then run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal, have the second Claude review the first Claude's work, start another Claude to read both the code and review feedback, and have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback. This separation often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything.
questions.question: In the multi-Agent verification pattern, what command do you use to start a fresh context in the same terminal for the second Claude to review the first Claude's work?
questions.explanation: The /clear command is used to reset the context window, allowing a fresh Claude session to review the previous work without carryover from the initial coding session.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Agent Workflows
questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees for Parallel Claude Sessions
questions.lessonContent: When using git worktrees to run multiple Claude sessions in parallel on different parts of your project, the workflow typically begins by creating a git worktree for one task. Once the worktree is created, you then launch Claude Code within that worktree directory. To scale this approach further, you would create additional worktrees in new terminal tabs and launch Claude sessions in each one. This allows each Claude instance to work independently on tasks like refactoring or building separate components without merge conflicts.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in setting up git worktrees for running multiple Claude sessions in parallel?

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.moduleTitle: Understanding Digital Images and Compression Basics
questions.lessonContent: Images look smooth and continuous, but when you zoom in far enough, you'll see they're made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers that represent how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create that specific color. Each of these color values can range from 0, which means none of that color, all the way up to 255, which represents the maximum intensity of that color. For example, an orange pixel might have values of rgb(255, 147, 41), meaning full red, moderate green, and low blue. This RGB system is the foundation of how digital images represent color on screens.
questions.question: What do the three numbers in each pixel represent?
questions.answer: how much red, green, and blue to mix together

questions.moduleTitle: Understanding Digital Images and Compression Basics
questions.lessonContent: A standard HD screenshot has dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels, which equals over 2 million total pixels in the image. Since each pixel needs 3 bytes of storage (one byte for red, one for green, and one for blue), the math works out to 2,073,600 pixels multiplied by 3 bytes equals 6,220,800 bytes, which is approximately 6.2 megabytes for a single uncompressed image. This large file size is why compression is necessary for storing and transmitting images efficiently. Without compression, images would require massive amounts of storage space and bandwidth.
questions.question: An HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels and 3 bytes per pixel equals approximately 6.2 megabytes.

questions.moduleTitle: Understanding Digital Images and Compression Basics
questions.lessonContent: There are two fundamental approaches to compressing image files: lossy compression and lossless compression. Lossy compression, used by formats like JPEG, throws away parts of the image that humans won't typically notice, such as fine color details that the human eye blurs together. Lossless compression, used by formats like PNG, preserves every single pixel perfectly while still shrinking the file size through clever encoding techniques. Lossy compression can achieve 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference, while lossless compression typically achieves 3x smaller files for photographs but can reach 10-50x compression for screenshots with large solid color regions.
questions.question: Which approach to image compression preserves every single pixel perfectly?
choices: Both lossy and lossless preserve every pixel
Neither approach can preserve every pixel
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that lossless compression (used by PNG) preserves every single pixel while still shrinking the file size, whereas lossy compression throws away data that humans won't notice.

questions.moduleTitle: Understanding Digital Images and Compression Basics
questions.lessonContent: PNG combines three key tricks in sequence to compress images without losing quality. First, filtering stores differences between pixels rather than the raw pixel values. Then, LZ77 replaces repeated patterns with references to save space. Finally, Huffman coding gives common values shorter binary codes. The result is a compressed image that preserves every single pixel perfectly.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the compression steps in PNG encoding?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: Reducing Data by Removing Details
questions.lessonTitle: Human Vision and JPEG Color Processing
questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression exploits how human vision works. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. You notice a blurry edge, but you won't notice if colors are slightly off. JPEG takes advantage of this by converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color, and it reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice the difference.
questions.question: According to the content, why does JPEG reduce color resolution?
questions.answer: Because human eyes don't notice slight color differences as much as brightness details

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: Reducing Data by Removing Details
questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression (used by JPEG) throws away the parts humans won't notice to shrink file size. The algorithm keeps smooth parts intact while discarding high-frequency details like sharp edges that are harder for the human eye to perceive. This process permanently removes data from the original image.
questions.question: With lossy compression, you can recover the original pixel data by decompressing the file.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: Reducing Data by Removing Details
questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients in the image, while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: In JPEG compression, which type of frequency components does the algorithm discard to reduce file size?
choices: High-frequency components (fine details like sharp edges)
questions.explanation: JPEG keeps low-frequency components (smooth gradients) and discards high-frequency components (fine details like sharp edges) because photographs are mostly smooth gradients and human eyes won't notice the missing fine details.

questions.lessonTitle: The Three Tricks of Lossless Compression
questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression preserves every single pixel while still shrinking file size. It uses three main tricks to achieve this. First, filtering or prediction stores differences between pixels instead of absolute values, since adjacent pixels are usually similar. Second, LZ77 finds repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with compact back-references. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently. These three techniques work together in sequence to compress images like PNG files without any loss of data.
questions.question: What are the three tricks that lossless compression uses to shrink file size while preserving every pixel?
questions.answer: Filtering/prediction, LZ77 pattern-finding, and Huffman coding

questions.lessonContent: LZ77 is a pattern-finding algorithm used in lossless compression. It maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data as it scans through the file. When it finds a sequence that matches something previously seen within this window, it replaces the repeated data with a compact back-reference indicating how far back to look and how many bytes to copy. This approach is particularly effective for images with large solid color regions or gradual gradients, where the same patterns appear repeatedly.
questions.question: LZ77 uses a 32 KB sliding window.

questions.lessonContent: Huffman coding assigns binary codes based on how frequently each value appears in the data. The most common values receive the shortest codes, while rare values get longer codes. For example, if the value 0 appears 60% of the time, it might receive just 1 bit (like "0"). A value appearing 25% of the time might get 2 bits (like "10"), while values appearing only 5-10% of the time receive 3 bits each (like "110" or "111"). This approach can make the overall data much smaller than using fixed-length codes for every value.
questions.question: Based on the example in the content, if a value appears 60% of the time, how many bits would Huffman coding assign to it?
questions.explanation: The content states that the value 0 (appearing 60% of the time) gets just 1 bit: 0. This demonstrates how Huffman coding gives the most common values the shortest codes.

questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression used by PNG preserves every single pixel while shrinking file size through three sequential tricks. First, filtering predicts each pixel from its neighbors and stores the differences rather than absolute values. Second, LZ77 finds repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with compact back-references. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values. These three techniques work together in sequence to achieve 3x-50x compression without losing any pixel data.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the three tricks used in PNG lossless compression?
choices: Huffman: Give common values shorter codes
LZ77: Replace repeated patterns with references

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire officially began in 30 BCE, following Octavian's victory over Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. Unlike the earlier Roman Republic which lasted from 509 BCE to 30 BCE, the Roman Empire was ruled by emperors beginning with Augustus. The Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus, meaning "most high," in 27 BCE. In 23 BCE, Augustus was made consul for life and received the title "Princeps," meaning "first citizen," which became the origin of the word "prince." He also received the title "Imperator," meaning "successful general," which became the origin of the word "emperor."
questions.question: When did the Roman Empire officially begin?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Augustus and later Roman emperors maintained the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators through the Latin phrase "primus inter pares," meaning "first among equals." This concept gave the illusion that an emperor was the most prestigious and important member of the Roman Senate, while simultaneously suggesting that each senator was equally important.
