In reality, Roman emperors ruled with little input from anyone else. Augustus held numerous powers including the ability to call the Senate, veto the Senate's laws, and make laws himself. He also held the title of Pontifex Maximus, meaning "chief religious leader," which is the origin of the word "pontiff" used to describe the pope today.
questions.question: The phrase "primus inter pares" was used by Roman emperors to show they were equal to ordinary citizens in power.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Augustus established a golden age for Rome by implementing numerous reforms and building projects. He attempted to reform public morals by promoting family life, established fire and police departments for Rome, and built and maintained the empire's infrastructure including roads. Augustus extended citizenship to more and more provincials and established a strong money system. He famously said he "found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble." The Pax Romana, or Roman Peace, was a period of nearly 200 years during which Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region with almost no warfare.
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT an accomplishment of Augustus during his reign?
choices: Transforming Rome from bricks to marble
questions.explanation: The Colosseum was built by Vespasian (69-79 CE), not Augustus. Augustus established fire and police departments, extended citizenship to provincials, and famously transformed Rome from a city of bricks to a city of marble.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation, Division, and the Byzantine Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Diocletian's Division of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian was the first Roman ruler in 100 years to properly restore order after a century of chaos following the death of Marcus Aurelius, which is known as the Crisis of the Third Century. Diocletian was an absolute ruler who ended all personal liberties and increased the bureaucracy for more effective administration. In 285 CE, he divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west), which was the first step in the creation of what would become two separate empires: the Roman (Western) Empire and the Byzantine (Eastern) Empire. Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen the empire, though this ultimately proved to be incorrect.
questions.question: In what year did Diocletian divide the Roman Empire into two administrative realms?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation, Division, and the Byzantine Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The End of the Byzantine Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire was created when the Roman Empire was divided into east and west administrative regions. While the Western (Roman) Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer, the Eastern Empire continued to exist. The Byzantine Empire, headquartered at Constantinople, lasted for nearly a thousand years after the fall of the Western Empire. The Byzantine Empire finally came to an end in 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks.
questions.question: The Byzantine Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation, Division, and the Byzantine Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Constantine and the Edict of Milan
questions.lessonContent: Constantine became emperor of the Roman Empire from 312 to 337 CE and made a pivotal decision that would shape the future of Christianity. His mother Helena had converted to Christianity, influencing his religious perspective. In 313 CE, Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, which legalized Christianity and established religious toleration throughout the empire. This was a crucial turning point for Christianity, which had previously faced persecution. Constantine later converted to Christianity on his deathbed, and future Roman emperors would also be Christians, leading to Christianity's eventual dominance in the empire.
questions.question: What did Constantine accomplish regarding Christianity?
choices: He made Christianity the mandatory religion for all Roman citizens
He banned all religions except Christianity
He issued the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, legalizing Christianity and establishing religious toleration
He founded Christianity as a new religion
questions.explanation: The Edict of Milan, issued in 313 CE, was a crucial proclamation that legalized Christianity and established religious toleration throughout the Roman Empire. This allowed Christianity to practice freely and eventually become the dominant religion of the empire.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation, Division, and the Byzantine Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Administrative Division and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE as part of his administrative reforms to strengthen governance. Later, Emperor Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople. Eventually, the Western Roman Empire ended in 476 CE when the last emperor Romulus Augustus was deposed by the barbarian Odoacer.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the administrative division and eventual fall of the Roman Empire?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The End of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. However, the Western (Roman) Empire ended much earlier. It ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event is traditionally considered the fall of Rome and the end of ancient history.
questions.question: In what year did the Western Roman Empire officially end?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: The Roman economy faced several critical problems that contributed to the empire's decline. There was a significant gap between the rich and the poor. Impoverished workers became tied to the land as coloni and were sold with the land. As fewer members of the lower classes could afford to buy goods due to lack of purchasing power, manufacturing and trade declined. Additionally, large estates became self-sufficient, further hurting manufacturing and trade.
questions.question: The economic reasons for Rome's fall included a growing gap between rich and poor and a decline in manufacturing and trade due to people having less purchasing power.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: The Romans made numerous lasting contributions to world civilization. In administration, Rome learned to adapt policies locally for diverse populations across an empire of over 100 million people. Christianity started in the Roman province of Judea and spread throughout the empire due to Roman infrastructure and citizenship rights. Roman architecture included aqueducts, bridges, dams, harbors, roads, amphitheaters, and the Colosseum. Roman law was codified in the Justinian Code and still forms the basis for civil law in many European countries. Romance languages including French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish developed from Latin.
questions.question: Which of the following is a lasting contribution of Roman civilization to world history?
choices: The invention of the printing press
The construction of the Great Wall of China
The development of Roman law, which still forms the basis for civil law in many European countries
The establishment of democracy in Rome
questions.explanation: The Justinian Code encapsulated over 1000 years of Roman law and is still used as the basis for civil law in many parts of Europe. The other options are incorrect as they are not Roman contributions.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After Emperor Nero committed suicide in 68 CE, the Roman Empire experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. First, the Senate appointed Galba as the new emperor. However, Otho soon overthrew Galba in a coup. Vitellius then defeated Otho in battle, becoming the third emperor that year. Finally, Vespasian defeated Vitellius and established a more stable rule that would last until 79 CE.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the succession of emperors during the Year of the Four Emperors?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonTitle: Definition and Core Components of Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent research system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The Research feature specifically involves an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. This architecture enables the system to handle open-ended research problems where it's difficult to predict required steps in advance. The dynamic, path-dependent nature of research tasks makes AI agents particularly well-suited, as they must operate autonomously for many turns and make decisions about which directions to pursue based on intermediate findings.
questions.question: What is a multi-agent system?
questions.answer: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.lessonTitle: Multi-Agent Research Systems Outperform Single-Agent Systems on Complex Queries
questions.lessonContent: According to Anthropic's internal evaluations, multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. Their testing showed that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research evaluation. For example, when asked to identify all the board members of the companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found the correct answers by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single agent system failed to find the answer with slow, sequential searches.
questions.question: A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on internal research evaluations.

questions.lessonTitle: Orchestrator-Worker Pattern in Multi-Agent Research Architecture
questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the entire research process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. Each subagent acts as an intelligent filter by iteratively using search tools to gather information on specific research tasks, then returning findings to the lead agent so it can compile a final answer. This differs from traditional Retrieval Augmented Generation approaches that use static retrieval, as the multi-agent architecture employs multi-step search that dynamically finds relevant information, adapts to new findings, and analyzes results to formulate high-quality answers.
questions.question: Which architectural pattern does Anthropic's Research system use?
choices: Pipeline pattern where agents process queries sequentially in stages
Mesh pattern where all agents communicate directly with each other
Hierarchical pattern where senior agents supervise junior agents
Orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates while delegating to specialized subagents
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states the Research system uses "a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel."

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation for Research Agents
questions.lessonContent: Parallel tool calling significantly improves research agent speed and performance. Anthropic's research system implements two types of parallelism: the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially, and subagents themselves use 3 or more tools in parallel. These parallelization changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries, allowing the Research system to accomplish more work in minutes instead of hours while covering more information than other systems.
questions.question: By what percentage did parallel tool calling reduce research time for complex queries?

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation for Research Agents
questions.lessonContent: Evaluating multi-agent research outputs programmatically is difficult since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. Anthropic found that LLMs are a natural fit for grading outputs. They used an LLM judge that evaluated outputs against criteria in a rubric including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. Testing showed that a single LLM call with one prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements, allowing scalable evaluation of hundreds of outputs.
questions.question: A single LLM call with one prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade produces evaluations that are consistent with human judgements.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation for Research Agents
questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically because they are free-form text with rarely a single correct answer. Anthropic addressed this by using an LLM judge that evaluated each output against multiple criteria in a rubric. The evaluation criteria included factual accuracy to verify whether claims match sources, citation accuracy to confirm cited sources match the claims, and completeness to check whether all requested aspects were covered.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a criterion used in Anthropic's LLM-as-judge evaluation rubric?
choices: Grammatical correctness (does the text follow proper syntax?)
Citation accuracy (do cited sources match the claims?)
questions.explanation: The three criteria explicitly mentioned in the source are factual accuracy, citation accuracy, and completeness. Grammatical correctness is not listed as a criterion in their evaluation rubric.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation for Research Agents
questions.lessonContent: When evaluating research agents, the team recommends starting with small evaluation samples immediately since changes in early agent development tend to have dramatic impacts with abundant low-hanging fruit. They began by testing with 20 queries representing real usage patterns, which allowed them to clearly see the impact of changes. This approach enables the identification of large effects quickly, as a single prompt tweak might boost success rates from 30% to 80%.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the recommended evaluation approach for research agents?

questions.lessonTitle: Rainbow Deployments for Stateful Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever deploying updates, agents might be anywhere in their research process. We cannot update every agent to the new version simultaneously without disrupting running agents. Instead, we use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: What deployment strategy does Anthropic use to prevent disrupting running agents when updating their multi-agent research system?

questions.lessonTitle: End-State Evaluation for Agents with Persistent State
questions.lessonContent: Evaluating agents that modify persistent state across multi-turn conversations presents unique challenges. Unlike read-only research tasks, each action can change the environment for subsequent steps, creating dependencies that traditional evaluation methods struggle to handle. We found success focusing on end-state evaluation rather than turn-by-turn analysis. Instead of judging whether the agent followed a specific process, we evaluate whether it achieved the correct final state. This approach acknowledges that agents may find alternative paths to the same goal while still ensuring they deliver the intended outcome.
questions.question: For agents that mutate state over many turns, Anthropic evaluates success by checking whether the agent achieved the correct final state, rather than judging whether it followed a specific prescribed process.

questions.lessonTitle: Memory Management Strategies for Long Conversations
questions.lessonContent: Production agents often engage in conversations spanning hundreds of turns, requiring careful context management strategies. As conversations extend, standard context windows become insufficient, necessitating intelligent compression and memory mechanisms. We implemented patterns where agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. When context limits approach, agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs. They can retrieve stored context like the research plan from their memory rather than losing previous work when reaching the context limit.
questions.question: Which memory management technique does Anthropic use when the context window approaches its limit during long-horizon agent conversations?
choices: Agents switch to a different LLM model with larger context
Agents summarize completed work and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks
Agents restart the conversation from the beginning to reset context
Agents delete all previous context and start fresh
questions.explanation: When context limits approach, agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. They can also spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs and retrieving stored context.

questions.lessonTitle: Maximum Context Length for M2-Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings offers state-of-the-art long context M2-Retriever models with varying context lengths to handle different document sizes. These models include M2-BERT retrieval options for 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths. The 32k context length model represents the longest context capability available, allowing users to generate embeddings for very long documents without splitting them into many short chunks. This enables more meaningful contexts to be contained within the embeddings.
questions.question: What is the maximum context length supported by M2-Retrieval models?

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings endpoint is available today with 8 open source embedding models. These include top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. Additionally, the platform offers newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context handling. The content explicitly states that these 8 models include models that outperform OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3 in MTEB and LoCo Benchmarks.
questions.question: Together Embeddings offers 8 leading embedding models, including top models from the MTEB leaderboard.

questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors is usually too large to easily visualize in two-dimensional space. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model specifically, the embedding dimension is 768. This means each text processed by this model produces a vector with 768 dimensions. When visualizing embeddings from this model, techniques like t-SNE are used to transform the 768-dimensional vectors into 2D for plotting.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768.

questions.lessonTitle: Introduction to Together Embeddings: Data Visualization Workflow
questions.lessonContent: When visualizing embeddings using the Together Embeddings endpoint, the process follows a specific sequence. First, the generate_embeddings function is called to send text data to the Together API and receive embedding vectors. Next, the embeddings must be extracted from the API response object, typically from the data field. Finally, these high-dimensional embeddings are transformed using tSNE to reduce them to 2D for visualization. This three-step process allows high-dimensional embedding data to be displayed as a scatter plot where similar texts appear near each other.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Together Embeddings data visualization pipeline?

questions.lessonTitle: Together Embeddings API Base URL Configuration
questions.lessonContent: When setting up the Together Embeddings endpoint in your Python application, you need to configure the OpenAI-compatible client with the correct base URL. The Together Embeddings endpoint uses the base URL "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" which allows for seamless migration from OpenAI's embedding API. This base URL is used in the client initialization along with your Together API key to make requests to the embeddings endpoint.
questions.question: What is the base URL for the Together Embeddings API endpoint?

questions.lessonTitle: OpenAI API Compatibility of Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was designed with full OpenAI compatibility to make migrating existing applications straightforward. This means if you have already built applications following the OpenAI API structure, you can easily switch to Together's endpoint by changing only the base URL and API key. The client initialization and method calls remain largely identical between OpenAI's implementation and Together's implementation, reducing the friction of switching providers.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint has full OpenAI API compatibility so that applications can easily migrate.

questions.lessonTitle: Model API String Format for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K
questions.lessonContent: When making embeddings requests to the Together API, you must specify the model using its API string. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model, the correct API string is "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval". This model is one of the M2-BERT retrieval models designed for long context retrieval tasks, supporting up to 8k context length. The API string is passed as the model parameter in the client.embeddings.create() method to specify which embedding model to use for generating embeddings.
questions.question: What is the correct API string to use when requesting embeddings from the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?
questions.explanation: The correct API string for the 8k context version of the M2-BERT retrieval model is "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval", which explicitly includes the 80M parameter size and 8k context length in its name.

questions.lessonContent: When implementing the Together Embeddings API, the process begins with defining a get_embedding function that prepares the input text, then calls the embeddings.create API to generate the embedding, and finally extracts the embedding vector from the response. This sequence ensures the text is properly formatted before API call, the embedding is generated through the Together API, and the resulting vector is correctly retrieved from the response object.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Together Embeddings API implementation process?

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG and Data Visualization Applications
questions.lessonContent: RAG stands for Retrieval Augmented Generation, which is a technique that aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models. These limitations include a lack of knowledge from unseen data. RAG works by finding relevant information from a given knowledge base through embeddings and then providing that information to a generative model. This allows the generative model to access and utilize information that was not part of its original training data.
questions.question: What does Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) aim to overcome in generative AI models?
questions.answer: A lack of knowledge from unseen data

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG and Data Visualization Applications
questions.lessonContent: You can build RAG systems using Together API along with popular vector databases and frameworks. The supported vector databases include MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. Additionally, RAG can be built by leveraging frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex. These tools provide integration pathways for connecting embeddings with retrieval systems.
questions.question: Which of the following frameworks can be used together with the Together Embeddings endpoint to build RAG systems?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly mentions that RAG can be built using frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex. These are the supported frameworks for RAG implementation with Together Embeddings.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG and Data Visualization Applications
questions.lessonContent: In the data visualization workflow using Together Embeddings, the process follows a logical sequence. First, you must define embedding functions that will handle the API calls. Then, you extract samples from your data files in JSONL format. Next, you generate embeddings using the Together API with your chosen model. After obtaining the embedding vectors, you apply tSNE transformation to reduce the high-dimensional embeddings (768 dimensions for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K) into 2D coordinates. Finally, you plot the visualization using matplotlib to see how your data points cluster together.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the data processing workflow for visualizing embeddings with tSNE?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed for agentic software engineering. The model demonstrates strong long-term planning and coding intelligence while maintaining the ability to efficiently solve problems for interactive use. According to the technical report, the model is trained in two distinct phases: first, continued pretraining to improve the model's knowledge and latent coding ability, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance through stronger reasoning, accurate multi-step execution, and coherence on long-horizon realistic coding problems.
questions.question: In how many distinct phases is Composer 2 trained?

questions.lessonTitle: Definition of a Software Engineering Agent Rollout
questions.lessonContent: Software engineering agents aim to autonomously act to solve a given task prompt. According to the background section of the technical report, given an environment (a codebase and an isolated container for code execution) along with a prompt giving the agent its task, an agent produces a rollout consisting of a series of actions. Each action makes one or more tool calls and yields responses. The tool calls may modify the underlying environment, and the result of a rollout is the final state of this environment.
questions.question: The result of a software engineering agent rollout is the final state of the environment.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 has access to a small set of general tools that allow it to read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and search the web. Its prompt includes a system message, the tool call format specification, recent file information, past user messages, and the current task. The most common end result of this process is a set of changes to files in the codebase environment, although there are many other common use cases such as answering questions, writing plans, resolving version control issues, or monitoring long-running jobs.
questions.question: Which of the following tools is NOT explicitly listed as available to Composer 2 in the background section?
choices: Read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase, and deploy applications
Read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and debug errors
Read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and search the web
Read and edit files, compile code, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and search the web
questions.explanation: The technical report explicitly states that Composer 2 has tools to 'read and edit files, run shell commands, search the codebase using grep or semantic search, and search the web.' The other options include tools like 'compile code' or 'debug errors' which are not explicitly listed.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 extends the Kimi K2.5 base model through a continued pretraining stage divided into three distinct phases. The first and most computationally intensive phase uses a 32k token sequence length. The second phase is a shorter long-context extension that expands the sequence length to 256k tokens. The third phase is a brief supervised fine-tuning phase targeting specific coding tasks. Training was performed using MXFP8 precision on NVIDIA B300s GPUs with the AdamW optimizer.
questions.question: What is the sequence length used in the bulk of continued pretraining compute?

questions.lessonTitle: Overlong Rollout Handling in RL Training
questions.lessonContent: The technical report discusses whether to mask rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length in reinforcement learning training. Several prior works had mixed results: some masking approaches showed limited effectiveness on long-tail reasoning tasks but increased accuracy in medium and short-length reasoning tasks, while other research found that overlong masking caused output length to grow too quickly. The report explicitly states that the researchers did not see benefits with overlong masking at small scale and opted not to mask rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length.
questions.question: Composer 2 does not mask rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length.

questions.lessonTitle: Nonlinear Length Penalty for RL Rewards
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 employs a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty formula to incentivize efficient behavior. The formula Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1 - q)) uses hyperparameters k and q to define the penalty's curvature. The input x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns in a rollout. This nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks achievable with few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks where an agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls.
questions.question: What does the input x in the nonlinear length penalty formula represent?
choices: The total number of tokens generated by the model
A weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns
The inverse of the reward magnitude
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that x is 'a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout.'

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. The benchmark reflects the true distribution of software engineering tasks while completely avoiding train-set contamination. Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 which scored 44.2%. This performance is competitive with frontier models like Opus 4.6 High (58.2%) and GPT-5.4 (63.9%). The benchmark evaluates models using specific metrics targeting code quality, execution efficiency, and interactive agent behavior in realistic settings.
questions.question: What percentage does Composer 2 achieve on CursorBench?

questions.lessonContent: The RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations. This decoupled service stack enables larger-scale global training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding. The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute. Each service can be scaled independently based on its specific requirements, allowing the system to handle the demanding computational needs of training large language models for software engineering tasks.
questions.question: The RL infrastructure uses a decoupled service architecture consisting of four services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations.

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications compared to public benchmarks. CursorBench has a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. At the same time, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: Compared to public benchmarks, how many lines does CursorBench have as its median for lines changed in reference diff?
questions.explanation: CursorBench has a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual, demonstrating substantially more extensive code modifications are required.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation, making it ideal for documenting bash commands, code style guidelines, testing instructions, and repository etiquette. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo or wherever you run claude from (named CLAUDE.md and checked into git, or CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignored), any parent of the directory where you run claude (useful for monorepos), any child of the directory where you run claude (Claude pulls these in on demand when working with files in those directories), and your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md which applies to all claude sessions.
questions.question: In which location would you place a CLAUDE.md file if you want it to apply to all your Claude Code sessions across different projects?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code is designed with a deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety, and by default it requests permission for any action that might modify your system. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: selecting "Always allow" when prompted during a session, using the /permissions command to add or remove tools, manually editing your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, and using the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Using the --allowedTools CLI flag to configure tool permissions in Claude Code will persist those permissions for future sessions.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code provides multiple ways to customize which tools Claude is allowed to use without prompting for permission each time. The four documented methods include selecting "Always allow" when prompted during an active session, using the /permissions command to add or remove specific tools like Edit or Bash(git commit:*), manually editing configuration files in .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, and using the --allowedTools CLI flag which applies only to the current session.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method for managing allowed tools in Claude Code?
choices: Selecting "Always allow" when prompted during a session
Using the /env environment variable to configure tool permissions
Using the /permissions command after starting Claude Code
questions.explanation: The /env environment variable is not mentioned as a method for managing allowed tools. The four documented methods are: Always allow prompts, /permissions command, manual settings.json editing, and the --allowedTools CLI flag.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When customizing Claude Code, you first create a CLAUDE.md file to document commands, code style, and project guidelines. After creating the file, you should tune your CLAUDE.md content by refining instructions and adding emphasis to improve how Claude follows your guidance. Finally, you set up bash tools by telling Claude the tool name with usage examples so it can leverage your custom scripts.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in setting up and customizing Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code supports a versatile workflow called 'explore, plan, code, commit' that suits many problems. In the first step, you ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs, providing either general pointers or specific filenames, but explicitly tell it not to write any code yet. The second step involves asking Claude to make a plan for how to approach the specific problem, and using the word 'think' triggers extended thinking mode which gives Claude additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly. These specific phrases are mapped directly to increasing levels of thinking budget: 'think' is less than 'think hard' which is less than 'think harder' which is less than 'ultrathink.' Each level allocates progressively more thinking budget for Claude to use. Without these first two steps, Claude tends to jump straight to coding a solution.
questions.question: What word should you use to trigger extended thinking mode in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code offers a safe YOLO mode that bypasses all permission checks using the --dangerously-skip-permissions flag, allowing Claude to work uninterrupted until completion. This mode works well for workflows like fixing lint errors or generating boilerplate code. However, letting Claude run arbitrary commands is risky and can result in data loss, system corruption, or even data exfiltration via prompt injection attacks. To minimize these risks, the documentation recommends using --dangerously-skip-permissions in a container without internet access.
questions.question: The --dangerously-skip-permissions flag should be used in a container without internet access to minimize security risks.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, and can connect to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. These connections can be configured in three ways: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that directory), in global config (available in all projects), or in a checked-in .mcp.json file which makes the tools available to anyone working in the codebase. For example, you can add Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json so that every engineer working on your repo can use these out of the box. When working with MCP, it can also be helpful to launch Claude with the --mcp-debug flag to help identify configuration issues.
questions.question: Which of the following is a valid way to configure MCP server connections in Claude Code?
choices: Using a .claude/mcp-servers.json file for project-specific configuration
Using global config available in all projects
Using project config available when running Claude Code in that directory
Using a checked-in .mcp.json file available to anyone in the codebase
questions.explanation: The content specifies three valid methods: project config, global config, and .mcp.json. The .claude/mcp-servers.json file is not mentioned in the source content and is therefore not a valid method.

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees for Parallel Claude Sessions
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. This enables running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project, each focused on its own independent task. For example, you might have one Claude refactoring your authentication system while another builds a data visualization component. Since the tasks don't overlap, each Claude can work at full speed without waiting for the other's changes. To create a worktree, you use the command 'git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a', then launch Claude in each worktree with 'cd ../project-feature-a && claude'.
questions.question: What Git command do you use to create a new worktree for parallel Claude sessions?

questions.lessonContent: A powerful multi-Claude workflow involves having one Claude instance write code while another reviews or tests it. The process involves five steps: first, use Claude to write code; second, run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal; third, have the second Claude review the first Claude's work; fourth, start another Claude or /clear again to read both the code and review feedback; fifth, have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback. You can also have your Claude instances communicate with each other by giving them separate working scratchpads and telling them which one to write to and which one to read from. This separation often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything.
questions.question: True or False: Claude instances can communicate with each other by using separate working scratchpads.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code headless mode enables programmatic integration into larger workflows using 'claude -p' with a prompt. There are two primary patterns for automation: fanning out and pipelining. Fanning out handles large migrations or analyses by having Claude write a script to generate a task list, then looping through tasks by calling Claude programmatically for each task. Pipelining integrates Claude into existing data or processing pipelines by calling 'claude -p "<your prompt>" --json | your_command', where your_command is the next step of your processing pipeline. For debugging Claude invocations, the --verbose flag can be helpful, though it should generally be turned off in production for cleaner output.
questions.question: Which of the following is a valid use case for fanning out with headless mode?
choices: Connecting to an MCP server for a quick task
Starting a new Claude session with specific permissions
Running a single interactive code review session
Analyzing sentiment in hundreds of log files or migrating thousands of files between frameworks
questions.explanation: Fanning out is specifically designed for handling large-scale tasks like analyzing hundreds of logs or migrating thousands of files, where you programmatically loop through tasks calling Claude for each one.

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees for Parallel Claude Sessions
questions.lessonContent: When using git worktrees to run multiple Claude sessions in parallel on different parts of your project, you first create a worktree for a specific task using the git worktree add command. Then you launch Claude Code in that worktree directory to start working on that isolated task. Once you're done with all your parallel work, you clean up the worktrees using git worktree remove to remove the directory and clean up the git metadata.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in setting up and running parallel Claude sessions using git worktrees?

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images look smooth and continuous, but zoom in far enough and you'll see they're made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together. Each value ranges from 0, meaning none of that color, to 255, meaning maximum intensity. For example, the color rgb(255, 147, 41) represents pure red at maximum, moderate green, and low blue. An HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels in total.
questions.question: What are the three numbers in each pixel of a digital image?

questions.lessonContent: An HD screenshot with dimensions 1920 × 1080 pixels contains exactly 2,073,600 pixels. Each pixel needs 3 bytes of storage, one byte each for the red, green, and blue color values. This means a single uncompressed HD image requires 2,073,600 multiplied by 3 bytes, which equals 6,220,800 bytes, approximately 6.2 megabytes. This large file size is why compression is essential for storing and transmitting images efficiently.
questions.question: An HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels and requires approximately 6.2 megabytes of storage when uncompressed.

questions.lessonContent: There are two fundamental approaches to shrinking image file sizes. The first approach is lossy compression, which throws away data that humans won't notice, trading some quality for significantly smaller file sizes. The second approach is lossless compression, which preserves every single pixel perfectly while still achieving size reduction through clever encoding. These two ideas power common image formats like JPEG and PNG, as well as ZIP files, web traffic, and most of the internet's data transmission. Lossy compression can achieve 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference, while lossless compression keeps all original data intact.
questions.question: What are the two fundamental approaches to image compression?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states there are two approaches: lossy compression throws away parts humans won't notice, while lossless compression is clever about how every pixel is stored.

questions.lessonContent: The PNG lossless compression pipeline uses three main techniques to reduce file size while preserving all pixel data. First, filtering predicts each pixel based on its neighbors and stores the differences, which are usually small numbers. Next, LZ77 pattern finding scans for repeated sequences in the filtered data and replaces them with compact references. Finally, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to more common values, further reducing the size. These steps transform the original image data into a compressed PNG file.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: Trading Quality for Size
questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details that humans won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact. This block-based approach is fundamental to how JPEG achieves its compression.
questions.question: In JPEG compression, images are divided into blocks of what size?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: Trading Quality for Size
questions.lessonContent: At high quality settings, you barely notice the difference between the original and compressed image. However, when you crank up the compression ratio, you'll see blocking artifacts where fine details get lost. These artifacts appear as visible squares or blocky patterns in areas where the high-frequency information has been discarded. The blocking effect occurs because JPEG processes the image in 8×8 blocks, and at high compression, the data discarded in each block becomes noticeable.
questions.question: When JPEG compression is set to very high levels, visible square patterns called blocking artifacts appear in the image.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: Trading Quality for Size
questions.lessonContent: With lossy compression, you cannot get the original pixels back once they've been discarded. However, the tradeoff is often worth it because files become 10-20 times smaller with minimal visible difference. For example, an uncompressed HD screenshot at 6.2 megabytes can be compressed to around 400 kilobytes at 50% quality while still looking acceptable. This massive reduction in file size makes lossy compression essential for storing and transmitting images over the internet.
questions.question: What is the typical file size reduction achieved by lossy compression with minimal visible difference?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that with lossy compression, you can achieve '10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference.'

questions.lessonTitle: LZ77 Sliding Window Size in PNG Compression
questions.lessonContent: The third trick in PNG lossless compression uses an algorithm called LZ77, which scans for repeated patterns in the data. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 kilobytes of data it has processed. When the algorithm finds a pattern that matches something within this 32 KB window, it replaces the repeated sequence with a compact back-reference that says 'go back X values and copy Y values.' This reference is much smaller than repeating the actual data values. For images with large areas of similar color, such as solid backgrounds or smooth gradients, this technique significantly reduces file size.
questions.question: What is the size of the sliding window used by LZ77 in PNG compression?

questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression, used by the PNG format, is designed for situations where every pixel must be perfectly preserved. Unlike lossy compression which throws away data that humans won't notice, lossless compression keeps all the original pixel data intact. This is essential for screenshots containing text, graphics with sharp edges, or any image where exact pixel reproduction matters. When you decompress a losslessly compressed image, you get exactly the same pixel values you started with. The tradeoff is that lossless files are larger than lossy files, but precision is guaranteed.
questions.question: PNG uses lossless compression, meaning every pixel from the original image is preserved exactly when the file is decompressed.

questions.lessonTitle: Compression Ratios for Different Image Types
questions.lessonContent: PNG lossless compression achieves different results depending on the type of image being compressed. For photographs with complex, varied pixel values, a 6.2 MB uncompressed image becomes approximately 2.1 MB after PNG compression, representing about a 3x reduction in size. However, screenshots with large regions of solid color compress much more efficiently. These types of images can achieve 10x to 50x compression ratios because the pixels are highly repetitive. The solid color backgrounds and uniform text areas create many opportunities for the compression algorithms to reduce redundant data.
questions.question: Which type of image typically achieves higher compression ratios in PNG: photographs or screenshots with large solid color regions?
choices: Screenshots with large solid color regions
questions.explanation: Screenshots with large solid color regions achieve 10-50x compression because they contain highly repetitive pixel data that the compression algorithms can reduce very efficiently, whereas photographs with complex, varied pixel data only achieve about 3x compression.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire existed from 30 BCE to 476 CE, following the Roman Republic which lasted from 509 BCE to 30 BCE. While Rome technically had an empire under the Roman Republic, the term specifically refers to the period when Rome was ruled by emperors, beginning with Augustus. This marks a fundamental shift from the republican system of government to imperial rule. The Roman Empire replaced the Roman Republic as the dominant political structure in the Mediterranean world.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Empire?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. The Senate gave him the name Augustus, meaning "most high." In 23 BCE, Augustus was made consul for life by the Senate and acquired the titles Princeps (meaning "first citizen," origin of the word "prince"), Imperator (meaning "successful general," origin of the word "emperor"), Pontifex Maximus (meaning "chief religious leader," origin of the word "pontiff"), and tribune. He possessed the power to call the Senate, veto Senate laws, and create laws himself.
questions.question: Octavian was given the title "Augustus" by the Senate after his victory at the Battle of Actium.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: When Octavian became Augustus in 23 BCE, the Senate granted him multiple significant titles that would establish the imperial system. He was made consul for life and given the title Princeps, meaning "first citizen," which became the origin of the word "prince." He was also given the title Imperator, meaning "successful general," which is the origin of the word "emperor." Additionally, Augustus was made Pontifex Maximus, meaning "chief religious leader," which is the origin of the word "pontiff" still used today to describe the pope.
questions.question: What does the title "Pontifex Maximus" mean?
questions.explanation: "Pontifex Maximus" literally means "chief religious leader" and is the origin of the word "pontiff" used to describe the pope today. This title was one of several Augustus received from the Senate in 23 BCE, along with Princeps and Imperator.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. Following this military victory, the Senate gave him the name 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high.' Then, in 23 BCE, Octavian (now referred to as Augustus) was made consul for life by the Senate.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's rise to become the first Roman Emperor?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Governance
questions.lessonContent: The Latin phrase primus inter pares translates to "first among equals." Augustus and later Roman emperors attempted to maintain the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators. Being "first among equals" gave the illusion that an emperor was the most prestigious and important member of the Roman Senate, while simultaneously creating the perception that each senator was equally important. In reality, the Roman emperors ruled with little input from anyone else, despite this pretense of equality.
questions.question: What does the Latin phrase "primus inter pares" mean in English?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Governance
questions.lessonContent: Tiberius was the stepson of Augustus and ruled from 14-37 CE. He was a capable general who extended the frontier in the north and strengthened the empire. However, he appeared to dislike ruling and gradually retired to the island of Capri. He also abolished the Assembly, consolidating his power.
questions.question: Tiberius extended the Roman frontier in the north and strengthened the empire during his reign.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Governance
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, meaning "Roman Peace," was a period of relative peace and stability in the Roman Empire. Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, and this complete control meant almost no warfare. This peace lasted nearly 200 years, from approximately 27 BCE to 180 CE. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the Pax Romana?
choices: A period when Rome had no military forces
A time when the Roman Empire stopped expanding
A period of economic depression and decline
A nearly 200-year period of peace when Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region
questions.explanation: The Pax Romana was specifically described as lasting nearly 200 years during which Rome controlled the Mediterranean region with almost no warfare.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event marked the end of ancient Rome's political dominance in the West. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire, however, continued to exist for nearly another millennium, lasting until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The split between the Eastern and Western empires began with Diocletian in 285 CE, who divided the empire into two administrative realms to strengthen administration. Once Constantine established Constantinople as a rival capital city, the division between east and west deepened significantly.
questions.question: When did the Western Roman Empire officially end?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Constantine played a pivotal role in the history of Christianity. His mother Helena had converted to Christianity before him. In 313 CE, Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, which legalized Christianity and granted religious toleration throughout the empire. Constantine eventually converted to Christianity on his deathbed. After Constantine, future Roman emperors were Christians, and Christianity gained acceptance as the favored religion of the Roman state.
questions.question: Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, which recognized Christianity as the official state religion of the Roman Empire.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Decline and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: The Romans made numerous lasting contributions to world civilization across multiple domains. In administration, Rome governed an empire of over 100 million people through a complex bureaucracy of proconsuls, governors, and officials. In law, the Justinian Code (Corpus Juris Civilis) compiled by Emperor Justinian in the 6th century became the basis for civil law in many European countries. In language, Romance languages including French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish all developed from Latin. Additionally, Roman engineering achievements including aqueducts, roads, bridges, and the Colosseum demonstrated exceptional practical application of architectural principles.
questions.question: Which of the following is a lasting contribution of Rome to world history?
choices: The invention of the printing press
The establishment of the Olympic Games
The creation of democracy as a political system
The development of Romance languages from Latin
questions.explanation: French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish all developed directly from Latin, making this a documented Roman contribution. The printing press was invented much later, democracy existed before Rome in Greece, and the ancient Olympic Games predated Rome.

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, which are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. Our Research feature uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. Each subagent acts as an intelligent filter by iteratively using search tools to gather information before returning findings to the lead agent for synthesis. This architecture enables parallel reasoning and exploration across multiple contexts.
questions.question: What architecture pattern does Anthropic's Research system use?

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems have significantly higher token consumption compared to single-agent chat interactions. In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. This increased token usage is necessary for economic viability—the value of the task must be high enough to pay for the increased performance. We found that multi-agent systems excel at valuable tasks that involve heavy parallelization, information that exceeds single context windows, and interfacing with numerous complex tools. The architecture distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chat interactions.

questions.lessonContent: In our analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, which tests the ability of browsing agents to locate hard-to-find information, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance. We found that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, making it the dominant factor. The number of tool calls and model choice were the two other explanatory factors. This finding validates our architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. The latest Claude models act as large efficiency multipliers on token use, as upgrading to Claude Sonnet 4 is a larger performance gain than doubling the token budget on Claude Sonnet 3.7.
questions.question: What percentage of performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation does token usage alone explain?
questions.explanation: Token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and model choice as the two other factors that together explain 95%.

questions.moduleTitle: Designing, Prompting, and Evaluating Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: When delegating tasks to subagents, the lead agent must provide each subagent with four essential components: an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information. In early tests, simple short instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage' were too vague, causing subagents to misinterpret tasks or perform identical searches as other agents. For instance, one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while two others duplicated work investigating current 2025 supply chains, without effective division of labor.
questions.question: What are the four components that must be included when delegating tasks to subagents?
questions.answer: An objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries

questions.moduleTitle: Designing, Prompting, and Evaluating Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Complex research tasks naturally involve exploring many sources. Early agents executed sequential searches, which was painfully slow. Anthropic introduced two kinds of parallelization: the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially, and the subagents use 3+ tools in parallel. These changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.
questions.question: Parallel tool calling reduced research time by up to 90% for complex queries.

questions.moduleTitle: Designing, Prompting, and Evaluating Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic used an LLM judge to evaluate research outputs against criteria in a rubric including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. Factual accuracy checks whether claims match sources, citation accuracy verifies cited sources match the claims, completeness assesses whether all requested aspects are covered, source quality evaluates whether primary sources were used over lower-quality secondary sources, and tool efficiency measures whether the right tools were used a reasonable number of times.
questions.question: Which of the following is a criterion included in Anthropic's LLM-as-judge evaluation rubric?
questions.explanation: Grammar correctness is not one of the five criteria. The evaluation rubric specifically uses: factual accuracy (claims match sources), citation accuracy (cited sources match claims), completeness (all requested aspects covered), source quality (primary over secondary sources), and tool efficiency (right tools used reasonably).

questions.moduleTitle: Designing, Prompting, and Evaluating Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: In the multi-agent research system, the workflow begins when a user submits a query. The lead agent then analyzes the query, develops a research strategy, and spawns specialized subagents to explore different aspects of the topic in parallel. Each subagent independently performs web searches and returns findings to the lead agent for synthesis.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Anthropic's multi-agent research system when it transitions from receiving a query to executing research?

questions.moduleTitle: Production Engineering: Reliability, Deployment, and Scale
questions.lessonTitle: Resuming from Checkpoints in Agentic Systems
questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, minor system failures can be catastrophic because agents are stateful and run for long periods of time across many tool calls. When errors occur, restarting from the beginning would be expensive and frustrating for users. Instead, Anthropic built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred. They also leverage the model's intelligence to handle issues gracefully—for example, letting the agent know when a tool is failing and allowing it to adapt. This combines the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: What mechanism do Anthropic's agents use to handle errors without restarting from the beginning?
questions.answer: Checkpoint-based recovery and resuming from where the agent was when errors occurred

questions.moduleTitle: Production Engineering: Reliability, Deployment, and Scale
questions.lessonTitle: Rainbow Deployments Prevent Disruption of Running Agents
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. When deploying updates, agents might be anywhere in their process, so well-meaning code changes could break existing agents. Updating every agent to the new version simultaneously would cause disruptions.
questions.question: Rainbow deployments involve updating all agents to a new version at the exact same time to ensure consistency.

questions.moduleTitle: Production Engineering: Reliability, Deployment, and Scale
questions.lessonContent: Production agents engage in conversations spanning hundreds of turns, requiring careful context management. As conversations extend, standard context windows become insufficient, necessitating intelligent compression and memory mechanisms. When context limits approach, agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs. They can retrieve stored context like the research plan from their memory rather than losing previous work when reaching the context limit. Which strategy do Anthropic's agents use to prevent context overflow in long conversations?
questions.question: Which strategy do Anthropic's agents use to prevent context overflow in long conversations?
choices: Summarizing completed work phases and storing essential information in external memory
Deleting all previous context and starting fresh
Compressing all previous messages into a single summary
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. This prevents context overflow while preserving conversation coherence across extended interactions.

questions.moduleTitle: Production Engineering: Reliability, Deployment, and Scale
questions.lessonTitle: Rainbow Deployment Process for Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: When deploying updates to agent systems, Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents. This approach involves first deploying the new agent version while keeping the old version running. The system then runs both versions simultaneously while gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions. Throughout this process, the team monitors agent behavior to ensure the new version performs correctly. Once they verify there is no disruption to running agents, they complete the traffic shift to finalize the deployment.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Anthropic's rainbow deployment process for agent systems?

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings offers state-of-the-art long context M2-Retrieval models that support varying context lengths. These models come in three configurations: 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths. The 32k model represents the longest context option available, allowing users to process very long documents without splitting them into many short chunks. This enables containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings while maintaining accuracy.
questions.question: What is the maximum context length supported by the M2-Retrieval models?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint includes newly released M2-BERT retrieval models designed for long context applications. According to the content, these M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. This superior performance allows users to generate embeddings for long documents while maintaining high accuracy and containing more meaningful contextual information.
questions.question: M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks.

questions.lessonContent: The embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model is 768 dimensions. The content explicitly mentions this specific dimension when discussing data visualization: "For M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768." This information is provided in the section explaining how to visualize sample data using tSNE to transform the high-dimensional embedding vectors into a 2D plot for visualization purposes.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768.

questions.lessonContent: The process of visualizing embeddings using the Together Embeddings endpoint follows a clear sequence. First, you read data from a JSONL file using Python's file handling capabilities. Next, you extract text samples from the data, ensuring each sample fits within the model's maximum context length. Finally, you generate embeddings via the Together API by calling the embeddings.create method with your extracted text samples. This three-step sequence of reading, extracting, and generating forms the foundation of the data visualization workflow before moving to dimensionality reduction and plotting.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Together Embeddings data visualization pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint features full OpenAI compatibility, allowing developers who have built applications following the OpenAI API to easily switch to Together's service. The API can be accessed by setting the base_url to "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" and using the Together API key. The client uses the openai library with OpenAI() initialization, then calls the create method on the embeddings endpoint. This compatibility makes migration straightforward for existing applications built on OpenAI's embedding API.
questions.question: What base URL should be specified when configuring the OpenAI client to use Together Embeddings?

questions.lessonTitle: RAG Integration with Vector Databases and Frameworks
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases for embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. Together API enables RAG implementation through integration with popular vector databases including MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. Additionally, developers can leverage RAG frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex to build retrieval-augmented applications. These integrations allow users to connect embeddings with external knowledge bases for improved generative AI responses.
questions.question: Together Embeddings supports RAG implementation with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex.

questions.lessonContent: When building a Retrieval Augmented Generation system with Together Embeddings, developers have multiple integration options available. The platform provides specific integrations with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for RAG implementations. Additionally, the documentation references support for other vector databases like Pinecone and Chroma. Each integration option enables connecting the Together Embeddings endpoint to a knowledge base for semantic retrieval.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT explicitly mentioned as an integration option for building RAG with Together Embeddings?
questions.explanation: While Pinecone is mentioned in the source content as a vector database option for RAG, the question asks what is NOT explicitly mentioned as an integration. Pinecone appears in the general RAG description, while MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex are specifically called out as integration options.

questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors is usually too large to easily visualize. For M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768. To plot each data example in 2D, we will use tSNE to transform the embedding vectors. The tSNE function takes parameters including n_components, perplexity, and random_state to transform high-dimensional embedding matrices into a lower-dimensional representation suitable for visualization.
questions.question: What technique is used to transform embedding vectors from high-dimensional space to 2D for visualization?

questions.lessonContent: In the data visualization example, embeddings from sample data sources including arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, github_sample.jsonl, and stackexchange_sample.jsonl were visualized using tSNE. The visualization revealed that texts from each data source are somewhat closely located. Additionally, we can observe similarities between github and stackexchange, and between book and c4, while github and book are less related.
questions.question: According to the data visualization example, texts from github and stackexchange show similarities, while github and book are less related.

questions.lessonContent: The data visualization pipeline uses the Together Embeddings endpoint with the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model to generate embeddings from sample data files. These embeddings are then transformed using tSNE for 2D visualization. The tSNE transformation requires specific parameters including n_components (set to 2 for 2D plotting) and perplexity, which controls the balance between local and global aspects of the data. In the main script example, perplexity is set to 15 when calling the plot_embeddings function.
questions.question: What perplexity value is used in the tSNE transformation within the data visualization script?
questions.explanation: The data visualization script explicitly sets perplexity=15 in the main script when calling plot_embeddings: plot_embeddings(embedding_ls, n_components=2, names=filenames, perplextiy=15)

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. It serves as an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, and developer environment setup. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo where you run claude from (the most common usage), any parent of the directory where you run claude (useful for monorepos), any child of the directory where you run claude, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: Where is the most common location for placing a CLAUDE.md file?
questions.answer: The root of your repo, or wherever you run claude from

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. This deliberately conservative approach prioritizes safety. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json (with the former recommended for team sharing), or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Claude Code was designed with a deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety. true or false?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: When creating CLAUDE.md files, you have two naming options depending on whether you want to share them with your team. You can name it CLAUDE.md and check it into git so that you can share it across sessions and with your team, which is the recommended approach.
