questions.lessonContent: There were two distinct periods of Roman government. The Roman Republic existed from 509 BCE to 30 BCE, while the Roman Empire spanned from 30 BCE to 476 CE. Rome technically had an empire during the Roman Republic, but the term 'Roman Empire' specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus, when Rome was ruled by emperors. Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, and the Senate gave him the name 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high'. In 23 BCE, Octavian was made consul for life by the Senate and assumed the titles of 'Princeps' (first citizen), 'Imperator' (successful general), 'Pontifex Maximus' (chief religious leader), and tribune.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
questions.answer: Roman Republic: 509 BCE-30 BCE; Roman Empire: 30 BCE-476 CE

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire - From Augustus to the Pax Romana
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, or Roman Peace, describes a period when Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, resulting in almost no warfare. This peace lasted nearly 200 years, from approximately 27 BCE to 180 CE. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship. The Pax Romana began under Augustus and continued through the reigns of Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero, Vespasian, Trajan, Hadrian, and Marcus Aurelius. The end of the reign of Marcus Aurelius (161-180 CE) marked the end of the Pax Romana.
questions.question: The Pax Romana was a period of almost 200 years of peace and stability throughout the Roman Empire.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire - From Augustus to the Pax Romana
questions.lessonContent: The quality of emperors who succeeded Augustus varied greatly. Tiberius (14-37 CE) was Augustus's stepson, a capable general who extended the empire's northern frontier and strengthened the empire, though he eventually retired to the island of Capri. Caligula (37-41 CE), son of Germanicus, earned his nickname 'little boots' from the Roman army as a child; he ruled effectively for two years before a severe illness led to two years of terrible rule involving the exile and killing of family members. Claudius (41-54 CE) brought southern Britannia under Roman control, opened the Senate to provincials, and conducted a census in 48 CE. Nero (54-68 CE), considered a tyrant, came to power after his mother allegedly poisoned Claudius and murdered his mother, stepbrother, two wives, and his teacher Seneca.
questions.question: Which of the following emperors was responsible for bringing southern Britannia under Roman control?
questions.explanation: Claudius brought southern Britannia (what later became Great Britain) under Roman control, as well as several kingdoms in the East. The other emperors did not undertake this conquest.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire - From Crisis to Collapse
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire fell due to multiple interconnected economic problems. A significant gap existed between the rich and poor, with impoverished workers becoming tied to the land as coloni who were sold alongside the land parcels. As fewer lower-class citizens could afford to purchase goods due to lack of purchasing power, manufacturing and trade declined throughout the empire. Additionally, large estates became increasingly self-sufficient, producing their own goods rather than participating in broader market trade, which further damaged manufacturing and commercial networks.
questions.question: What economic factor involved impoverished workers being sold as part of the land they worked?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire - From Crisis to Collapse
questions.lessonTitle: Military Loyalty in the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: During the Roman Republic, armies served Rome as a unified state. However, under the Roman Empire, armies gained the power to make and unake emperors based on their support. The empire increasingly relied on barbarian troops who were not ultimately loyal to Rome and could not be counted on to fight their fellow barbarians. These mercenary forces were primarily interested in obtaining booty rather than defending Rome or advancing Rome's strategic interests.
questions.question: True or false: Under the Roman Empire, armies were primarily interested in defending Rome rather than obtaining booty.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire - From Crisis to Collapse
questions.lessonTitle: Causes of the Western Roman Empire's Fall
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire fell due to political, military, economic, and social factors. Politically, there was no orderly succession system, with murders, forced suicides, and civil wars frequently accompanying transitions between emperors. The East/West split created loyalty problems as the empire divided into two separate entities. Socially, population declined from hunger, plagues, and war, while people abandoned public service and intellectual pursuits to watch chariot races and gladiatorial contests. Religious divisions emerged as Christianity and Eastern cults challenged traditional Roman religion and the concept of imperial divinity.
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a social reason for the Western Roman Empire's fall?
choices: Increase in public service and intellectual pursuits
Population decline from hunger, plagues, and war
questions.explanation: The content states that people 'did not dedicate themselves to public service and intellectual pursuits' - meaning there was a decline, not an increase. The other options (religious divisions, population decline from multiple causes) are explicitly listed as social reasons for Rome's fall.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire - From Crisis to Collapse
questions.lessonTitle: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After the Pax Romana ended with the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE, the Roman Empire entered a period of severe instability known as the Crisis of the Third Century. This era was marked by civil wars, economic collapse, and multiple emperors ruling simultaneously. Emperor Diocletian responded by dividing the empire into two administrative halves in 285 CE, creating separate Eastern and Western empires to make governance more manageable. Later, Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople, which further shifted power eastward. These administrative divisions ultimately contributed to the Western Empire's collapse in 476 CE when the last emperor was deposed.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the administrative fragmentation that led to the fall of the Western Roman Empire?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Roman Contributions to World History - Legacy of Civilization
questions.lessonContent: The Latin language developed into several modern "Romance" languages (meaning "Roman") across Europe. These include French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish. English, while originally a Germanic language, was significantly influenced by French following the Norman Conquest of 1066, when William the Conqueror brought French (a Romance language) to England. Modern English is a mixture of these old Germanic and French languages, with approximately half of its vocabulary tracing back to Latin. The Catholic Church also played a crucial role in preserving the Latin language, continuing to use it in masses until the 1960s.
questions.question: What are the five Romance languages that developed from Latin?
questions.answer: French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Roman Contributions to World History - Legacy of Civilization
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Justinian of the Byzantine Empire rewrote Roman law into what is known as the Corpus Juris Civilis, or the Justinian Code. This legal compilation encapsulated more than a thousand years of Roman legal development, including decisions of judges, ideas of the Republic and Empire, and rulings of emperors. The Justinian Code addressed public law (relationship of citizen to state), private or civil law (relationships between people), and peoples law (rights of foreigners). This comprehensive legal framework still forms the basis for civil law in many parts of Europe today.
questions.question: The Justinian Code (Corpus Juris Civilis) is still used as the basis for civil law in many parts of Europe today.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Roman Contributions to World History - Legacy of Civilization
questions.lessonContent: The Romans made numerous lasting contributions to world civilization. Their administration successfully managed an empire of over 100,000,000 diverse people through a strong bureaucracy of proconsuls, governors, and officials. They developed comprehensive Roman law starting with the Twelve Tables in 450 BCE, which evolved over a thousand years. In architecture and engineering, they built aqueducts, bridges, roads, and public buildings like the Colosseum, adapting the Greek style, Etruscan arch, and developing domes and vaults. They preserved and transmitted Greek (Hellenistic) culture to the West through the Catholic Church after Rome fell. Additionally, Christianity originated in the Roman province of Judea and spread throughout the empire thanks to Roman infrastructure and citizenship rights.
questions.question: Which of the following was a major contribution of Roman civilization to world history?
choices: Roman law and the Justinian Code, which influenced European legal systems
The complete destruction of Greek cultural texts
The establishment of democracy as Rome practiced it
The creation of the Japanese writing system
questions.explanation: Roman law, beginning with the Twelve Tables and culminating in the Justinian Code, is directly stated in the source content as a major contribution that still forms the basis for civil law in many parts of Europe. The other options are incorrect: the Romans preserved Greek culture rather than destroying it; democracy did not exist in reality in Rome; and the Romans had no connection to creating the Japanese writing system.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Roman Contributions to World History - Legacy of Civilization
questions.lessonTitle: The Division and Legacy of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The process of dividing the Roman Empire began when Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE. This created separate Eastern and Western administrations for more effective governance. Later, Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople, which further solidified the East-West division. Once Constantinople was established as a capital city, the divide between the Eastern and Western empires continued to deepen over time.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the administrative and geographical division of the Roman Empire?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, which are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The Research feature involves an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. Each subagent operates with its own context window and explores different aspects of a question before condensing the most important findings for the lead research agent. This architecture allows for independent, parallel investigations that reduce path dependency.
questions.question: What is a multi-agent system?
questions.answer: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems require significantly higher token usage compared to single-agent approaches. In practice, agents typically use about 4 times more tokens than standard chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15 times more tokens than chats. This increased token usage is necessary because subagents operate in parallel with their own context windows, exploring different aspects of questions simultaneously. The trade-off is that multi-agent systems excel at valuable tasks involving heavy parallelization and information that exceeds single context windows, making the higher token cost worthwhile for complex research tasks.
questions.question: Multi-agent research systems use approximately 15 times more tokens than standard chat interactions.

questions.lessonContent: Our Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the entire research process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information before returning their findings to the lead agent for synthesis. This differs from traditional Retrieval Augmented Generation approaches that use static retrieval, whereas our architecture uses multi-step search that dynamically finds relevant information, adapts to new findings, and analyzes results to formulate high-quality answers.
questions.question: Which architecture pattern does Anthropic's Research system use?
choices: Orchestrator-worker pattern with lead agent and subagents
Single agent with sequential tool calling
questions.explanation: The Research system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Agent Effort to Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: Effective prompt engineering requires matching agent resources to task difficulty. Anthropic embedded scaling rules in their prompts to help agents judge appropriate effort levels. Simple fact-finding queries require just one agent with three to ten tool calls. Direct comparisons might need two to four subagents with ten to fifteen calls each. Complex research tasks might use more than ten subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions.
questions.question: According to the prompt engineering principles, how many subagents should a lead agent use for a complex research task that requires dividing responsibilities among many specialized areas?

questions.lessonTitle: Parallel Tool Calling Improves Research Speed
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic implemented two types of parallelization to dramatically improve research speed. The lead agent spins up three to five subagents in parallel rather than serially, and the subagents themselves use three or more tools in parallel. These changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries, allowing the Research system to do more work in minutes instead of hours while covering more information than other systems. This parallel approach transformed both speed and performance of the multi-agent research system.
questions.question: Parallel tool calling reduces research time by up to 90% for complex queries.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic provided their agents with explicit heuristics for tool selection because agent-tool interfaces are as critical as human-computer interfaces. The key heuristics include examining all available tools first, matching tool usage to user intent, searching the web for broad external exploration, and preferring specialized tools over generic ones. Bad tool descriptions can send agents down completely wrong paths, so each tool needs a distinct purpose and a clear description. Using the right tool is often strictly necessary for task success, such as an agent searching the web for context that only exists in Slack being doomed from the start.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the tool selection heuristics that Anthropic embedded in their agent prompts?
choices: Always prioritize the most recently added tools
Prefer specialized tools over generic ones
Match tool usage to user intent
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states the heuristics include examining all available tools first, matching tool usage to user intent, and preferring specialized tools over generic ones. Prioritizing the most recently added tools is not mentioned as a heuristic.

questions.lessonContent: Effective evaluation of multi-agent systems requires a layered approach. First, you should start with small samples in early agent development because changes tend to have dramatic impacts and large effect sizes can be spotted with just a few test cases. Once you've refined initial prompts, you implement LLM-as-judge evaluation to scalably evaluate hundreds of outputs against criteria like factual accuracy and citation quality. Finally, you add human evaluation to catch edge cases that automation misses, such as hallucinated answers on unusual queries or subtle source selection biases.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent system evaluation strategy?

questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. They experimented with multiple judges but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.
questions.question: What numeric range does Anthropic's LLM judge use to score research outputs?

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever Anthropic deploys updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. They use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents during updates.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's LLM-as-judge evaluation uses multiple criteria to assess research outputs. The rubric includes factual accuracy which checks if claims match sources, citation accuracy which verifies that cited sources match the claims, completeness which determines if all requested aspects are covered, source quality which checks if the agent used primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources, and tool efficiency which evaluates if the agent used the right tools a reasonable number of times.
questions.question: Which of the following IS one of the evaluation criteria used by Anthropic's LLM-as-judge rubric?
questions.explanation: Writing style quality is not one of the evaluation criteria. The actual criteria are factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's evaluation approach for multi-agent systems follows a systematic progression. They begin by testing with small samples of about 20 queries representing real usage patterns, which allows them to spot dramatic impacts from changes when there is abundant low-hanging fruit. After identifying initial impacts, they scale evaluation using LLM-as-judge to evaluate hundreds of outputs against criteria like factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. Finally, human evaluation is applied to catch edge cases that automation misses, such as hallucinated answers on unusual queries, system failures, or subtle source selection biases that automated evals cannot detect.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the progressive agent evaluation workflow?
choices: Apply human evaluation for edge cases

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released on January 11, 2024. It provides access to 8 leading embedding models, including top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. Additionally, the endpoint includes newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context with different context lengths (2k, 8k, and 32k). These models achieve state-of-the-art performance in MTEB, showing comparable or even better accuracies than closed models.
questions.question: How many embedding models are available in the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was designed with full OpenAI API compatibility to make migrating easy for developers who have already built applications following the OpenAI API. Users can easily switch their existing applications by changing the base URL to "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" while using similar function calls. This compatibility is one of the key features that differentiates Together Embeddings from other embedding providers.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers full OpenAI API compatibility.

questions.lessonTitle: Available Context Length Options for M2-BERT Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: The M2-BERT retrieval models are specifically designed for long context tasks and significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. These models allow users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while retaining more meaningful contexts in the embeddings. The M2-BERT retrieval models are available in three context length options: 2k, 8k, and 32k, giving users flexibility to choose based on their document lengths and performance requirements.
questions.question: Which of the following is an available context length option for the M2-BERT retrieval models?
questions.explanation: The M2-BERT retrieval models are available in three context length options: 2k, 8k, and 32k. The 32k option provides the longest context capability among the choices listed.

questions.lessonContent: In this example, we first generate embeddings using the Together API for sampled data. Since embedding vectors have high dimensionality (768 dimensions for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K), we then transform these embeddings using tSNE to reduce them to 2 components for visualization. Finally, we visualize the transformed embedding vectors to see how data from different sources clusters together.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Together Embeddings visualization process?

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings supports integration with popular frameworks for building RAG applications. Beyond vector databases, developers can leverage LangChain and LlamaIndex to construct RAG systems. These frameworks provide abstractions for document loading, text splitting, embedding generation, and vector storage. Tutorials are available for building RAG using Together with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex.
questions.question: Name the two frameworks mentioned for building RAG with Together Embeddings.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors is usually too large to easily visualize. For M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768. This high-dimensional representation captures rich semantic information but requires dimensionality reduction techniques like tSNE for visualization purposes. When plotting embeddings in 2D, the code transforms the 768-dimensional vectors using tSNE with a perplexity of 15.
questions.question: The embedding dimension for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K is 768.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonTitle: Vector Databases for RAG with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases of embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. You can build RAG using the Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. Additionally, you can leverage frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex to simplify the RAG implementation process. These tools provide integration capabilities that make it straightforward to connect Together Embeddings with your preferred vector storage solution.
questions.question: Which of the following is a vector database option mentioned for building RAG with Together Embeddings?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly mentions MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma as vector database options for building RAG with Together Embeddings. Weaviate is not mentioned in the content.

questions.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The embedding dimension of M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K is 768, which is too large to easily visualize in its raw form. To plot each data example in 2D, the code uses tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform the embedding vectors. The transform_tSNE function takes parameters including n_components (number of output dimensions), perplexity (which controls the balance between local and global aspects of the data), random_state (set to 42 for reproducibility), and init. In the main script, the perplexity is set to 15 when calling plot_embeddings.
questions.question: What is the perplexity value used in the main script when running tSNE for data visualization?

questions.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases and Data Visualization
questions.lessonTitle: Data Source Relationships in Embedding Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The data visualization example uses sample data from RedPajama-v1, which includes various domains such as arxiv, book, c4, github, and stackexchange. After running the tSNE visualization, the results show that texts from each data source are somewhat closely located in the 2D space, indicating semantic similarity within domains. The visualization also reveals specific relationships: github and stackexchange data appear similar to each other, and book and c4 data show similarities. Conversely, github and book data are less related based on their distance in the visualization.
questions.question: According to the visualization results, github and book data are less related to each other than github and stackexchange data.

questions.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases and Data Visualization
questions.lessonTitle: Maximum Character Limit for Embedding Extraction
questions.lessonContent: When extracting samples from the data file for embedding generation, the code calculates the maximum number of characters to process based on the model's context length. The sample_and_extract_embeddings function uses max_num_chars = context_length * 4, based on the assumption that each token is approximately 4 characters. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model with context_length of 8192, this results in a max_num_chars value of 32,768 characters per sample.
questions.question: How is the maximum number of characters calculated in the sample_and_extract_embeddings function?
questions.explanation: The code explicitly states max_num_chars = context_length * 4, assuming each token is about 4 characters long.

questions.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The data visualization process with embeddings involves several key steps. First, you need to define data functions to handle the extraction and processing. Then, you sample and extract the data from your dataset, filtering based on context length requirements. Finally, you transform the high-dimensional embedding vectors using tSNE to create a 2D representation suitable for plotting.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Data Visualization with Embeddings process?

questions.lessonTitle: Purpose of Continued Pretraining in Composer 2
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage in Composer 2 aims to improve the language model's base knowledge specifically in the domain of coding. This stage provides a specialized base model for the subsequent agentic reinforcement learning training by specializing the model on coding knowledge and capabilities. The training extends Kimi K2.5 with a continued pretraining stage on a large code-dominated data mix. Continued pretraining has long been demonstrated to drastically improve downstream performance, and additional supervised learning reliably improves knowledge benchmarks and leads to improved coding performance of the final coding agent.
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the continued pretraining stage in Composer 2?
questions.answer: To improve the language model's base knowledge in coding and provide a specialized base model for subsequent agentic RL training

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 divides its continued pretraining stage into three distinct phases. The first and most computationally intensive phase runs at 32k token sequence length. This is followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. Finally, there is a short supervised fine-tuning phase focused on targeted coding tasks. During training, the evaluation loss on their internal codebase decreases log-linearly over the course of the training run, demonstrating steady improvement.
questions.question: True or False: The continued pretraining stage in Composer 2 consists of three phases, with the bulk of compute spent at 32k token sequence length followed by extension to 256k tokens.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 selected Kimi K2.5 as their base model, which is a 1.04T parameter model with 32B active parameters in a Mixture-of-Experts configuration. The selection was based on internal evaluations measuring three key metrics: coding knowledge tested with FreshBench (a question-answer benchmark), state tracking ability measured through an internal benchmark similar to LoCoDiff, and codebase perplexity measured on their private monorepo. Kimi K2.5 achieved 83.2% on FreshBench, a state tracking score of 86, and 13.81M negative log-likelihood, demonstrating strong performance across all three evaluation criteria.
questions.question: Based on the internal evaluations, which of the following models was selected as the base model for Composer 2?
questions.explanation: Kimi K2.5 was selected because it achieved strong performance across all three evaluation criteria: 83.2% on FreshBench coding knowledge benchmark, state tracking score of 86, and 13.81M negative log-likelihood on codebase perplexity, along with additional infrastructure efficiency considerations.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage aims to improve the language model’s base knowledge in coding. We first select a base model, which in this case was Kimi K2.5, using internal evaluations measuring codebase perplexity, coding knowledge, and state tracking. We then extend the base model with continued pretraining on a large code-dominated data mix to specialize the model on coding knowledge and capabilities. Finally, we apply a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks to prepare the model for downstream RL performance.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 continued pretraining process?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained by reinforcement learning on a large set of coding tasks. These tasks are run in environments that emulate real Cursor sessions. We create a problem distribution that reflects the most common use cases. Figure 3 shows the breakdown in terms of task category. The RL training tasks include: Iterate On Feature, Debugging, New Feature, Refactor, Understanding Codebase, Documentation, Testing, Code Review, Optimize, Devops, Migration, Deletion, and Other. Notably, our training distribution captures many aspects of software engineering absent from popular AI coding benchmarks.
questions.question: How many distinct task categories are included in Composer 2's RL training task distribution?

questions.lessonContent: Similar to prior work, we use a Kullback–Leibler divergence for regularization, KL(q∥p) = Ex∼q[−log r(x)], r(x) = p(x)/q(x). Many open-source implementations of RL estimate KL with the estimator k3 = (r −1) −log r. The k3 estimator is an unbiased estimator of KL and reduces variance when p and q are close. However, Amini et al. shows that the variance increases drastically as p and q diverge. See Figure 4: for large KL values, the variance of the estimate is extremely large. Therefore, we use the standard estimator k1 = −log r instead.
questions.question: True or False: Composer 2 uses the k3 KL divergence estimator because it reduces variance when p and q are close.

questions.lessonContent: To incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests, we add a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to the reward. The formula is: Clength{k,q}(x) = (1 + kx)1−q −1 / (k(1 −q)), where k and q are hyperparameters which define the curvature of the penalty, and the input x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout. The nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks, achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks, where the agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls.
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct formula for the nonlinear length penalty used to incentivize efficient agent behavior?
questions.explanation: The correct formula is Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)), where k and q are hyperparameters defining the curvature, and x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns.

questions.lessonContent: In Composer 2's reinforcement learning training, the process begins with sampling a problem from our task distribution, then simulating a group of rollouts from the agent with different solutions, and finally updating the model weights based on solution quality. This sequential pipeline ensures the model learns from diverse approaches to coding tasks.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 reinforcement learning training pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. Unlike public benchmarks, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed. In contrast, SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Multilingual have a median of only 7-10 lines changed per task. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering, where developers must synthesize context from production logs, sparse user bug reports, and large existing codebases.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks?

questions.lessonContent: Existing coding evaluations predominantly measure functional correctness. However, in practice, developers heavily weigh code quality, readability, latency, cost, and the quality of the agent's interactive behavior throughout a session. This narrow evaluation scope means that functional correctness alone does not capture the full spectrum of developer needs when using coding agents.
questions.question: True or False: Existing coding evaluations predominantly measure functional correctness, without considering code quality, readability, latency, cost, and interactive behavior.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services that enable large-scale training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding. The training service uses a fully asynchronous, high-throughput training stack built on Ray and PyTorch. The environments service runs stateful codebase environments on Anyrun, an internal compute platform. The inference service is partnered with Fireworks AI to run RL inference. The evaluations service runs pinned versions of the production backend for faithful model evaluations during training.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four decoupled services in Composer 2's RL infrastructure?
questions.explanation: The four decoupled services are training, environments, inference, and evaluations. 'Kimi K2.5 model training' is not a service—it is the base model used. The other three options are the actual services.

questions.lessonContent: To run faithful evaluations during training, Composer 2 follows a specific infrastructure process. First, for each training step we want to evaluate, we acquire a lease for an evaluation deployment. Then, the system automatically moves GPUs to that deployment. Finally, a cross-region weight sync of the evaluation checkpoint is performed from the training cluster where it resides to the inference deployment. This ensures the evaluation uses the exact same backend and weights as the production system.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 online evaluation deployment process?
choices: Cross-region weight sync from training cluster

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code provides special files that automatically get pulled into context when starting a conversation. These files are called CLAUDE.md files and serve as an ideal place for documenting bash commands, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, developer environment setup, and other information you want Claude to remember. When you run the /init command in Claude Code, it will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md file for you based on your project context. You can place CLAUDE.md files in the root of your repo, any parent or child directory of where you run claude, or in your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. The /init command provides a quick way to set up this configuration file without manually creating it.
questions.question: Which command automatically generates a CLAUDE.md file for your project?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code is designed with a deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety. By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. This conservative default ensures that users have control over potentially dangerous operations. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: selecting "Always allow" when prompted during a session, using the /permissions command after starting Claude Code, manually editing your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json files, and using the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: True or False: By default, Claude Code allows all tools without requesting permission.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation, making it ideal for documenting project-specific information. There are several locations where you can place CLAUDE.md files to customize your Claude Code environment. You can place a CLAUDE.md file in the root of your repo (the most common usage), which you can name CLAUDE.md and check into git to share across sessions with your team, or name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it. You can also place CLAUDE.md files in any parent directory of where you run claude (useful for monorepos) or any child directory (which Claude will pull in on demand when working with files in those directories). Additionally, you can place a CLAUDE.md file in your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies to all your claude sessions.
questions.question: Where can CLAUDE.md files be placed?
choices: Only in parent directories of where you run claude
Only in the root of your repository
In the repo root, parent directories, child directories, or your home folder (~/.claude/)
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that CLAUDE.md files can be placed in multiple locations: the root of your repo, any parent directory of where you run claude, any child directory, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. This flexibility allows for different configurations in monorepos and personal setups.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: When customizing your Claude Code setup, you first need to create CLAUDE.md files to document commands, code style, and project guidelines. After creating these files, you should tune your CLAUDE.md content by refining instructions and iterating on their effectiveness. Finally, you curate Claude's list of allowed tools to permit additional tools that you know are safe for your workflow.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in customizing your Claude Code setup?

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude's Capabilities and Mastering Common Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Custom slash commands are stored as Markdown files in the .claude/commands folder and become available through the slash commands menu when you type /. These commands can include the special keyword $ARGUMENTS to pass parameters from command invocation. For example, placing a command file at .claude/commands/fix-github-issue.md with content containing $ARGUMENTS makes the /project:fix-github-issue command available, and running /project:fix-github-issue 1234 would pass "1234" as the argument. You can also add personal commands to ~/.claude/commands for commands you want available in all sessions. Custom slash commands can be checked into git to share them with your team.
questions.question: What keyword is used in custom slash command files to pass parameters from command invocation?

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude's Capabilities and Mastering Common Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can connect to MCP servers in three ways: in project config when running Claude Code in that directory, in global config for availability in all projects, or in a checked-in .mcp.json file available to anyone working in the codebase. When working with MCP, it can be helpful to launch Claude with the --mcp-debug flag to help identify configuration issues. For example, you can add Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json so that every engineer working on your repo can use these out of the box.
questions.question: True or False: MCP servers configured in a checked-in .mcp.json file are available only to the person who configured them.

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude's Capabilities and Mastering Common Workflows
questions.lessonTitle: Workflow for Test-Driven Development with Claude
questions.lessonContent: The TDD workflow for using Claude Code consists of four distinct steps. First, ask Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs while explicitly stating you're doing test-driven development so it avoids creating mock implementations. Second, tell Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail without writing any implementation code. Third, ask Claude to commit the tests when satisfied. Fourth, ask Claude to write code that passes the tests without modifying them, instructing it to keep going until all tests pass. Claude performs best when it has a clear target to iterate against, and at this stage, asking it to verify with independent subagents can help ensure the implementation isn't overfitting to the tests.
questions.question: In the test-driven development workflow with Claude Code, at which step should you ask Claude to verify with independent subagents that the implementation isn't overfitting to the tests?
choices: Before running the tests for the first time
After writing code that passes the tests
questions.explanation: The correct answer is after writing code that passes the tests, because at that stage it helps to have Claude verify with independent subagents that the implementation isn't overfitting to the tests.

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude's Capabilities and Mastering Common Workflows
questions.lessonContent: The multi-Claude verification workflow uses multiple Claude instances to improve code quality through independent review. First, you use Claude to write code, then run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal. After that, have the second Claude review the first Claude's work. Next, start another Claude (or /clear again) to read both the code and review feedback. Finally, have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback, completing the verification process.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-Claude verification workflow?

questions.lessonContent: The multi-Claude verification workflow involves having one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it. First, use Claude to write code. Then, run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal. Have the second Claude review the first Claude's work. Next, start another Claude (or /clear again) to read both the code and review feedback. Finally, have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback. This separation often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything, as the separate contexts allow for independent evaluation.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-Claude verification workflow?
questions.answer: Use Claude to write code, run /clear or start a second Claude, have the second Claude review the work, start another Claude to read both code and feedback, then have this Claude edit the code based on feedback

questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files, while sharing the same Git history and reflog. This means you can run multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project, each focused on its own independent task. For example, you might have one Claude refactoring your authentication system while another builds a completely unrelated data visualization component. Since the tasks don't overlap, each Claude can work at full speed without waiting for the other's changes or dealing with merge conflicts.
questions.question: True or False: Git worktrees share the same Git history and reflog but have isolated working directories.

questions.lessonContent: Headless mode with a custom harness integrates Claude Code programmatically into larger workflows using two primary patterns. The first pattern called fanning out handles large migrations or analyses by having Claude write a script to generate a task list, then looping through tasks calling Claude programmatically for each task with specific instructions and allowed tools. The second pattern called pipelining integrates Claude into existing data or processing pipelines by calling claude -p with a prompt and piping the JSON output to another command. For fanning out, you would give each task explicit success/failure criteria like returning 'OK' if succeeded or 'FAIL' if the task failed.
questions.question: Which headless mode pattern involves generating a task list and looping through tasks calling Claude programmatically for each?
questions.explanation: Fanning out is the pattern that involves generating a task list (e.g., a list of files to migrate) and then looping through tasks, calling Claude programmatically for each individual task with specific instructions and allowed tools.

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images look smooth and continuous when viewed from a distance, but zoom in far enough and you'll see they are made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create that specific color. Each of these three color values can range from 0, meaning none of that color, to 255, representing the maximum intensity of that color. For example, the RGB values (255, 147, 41) create a specific shade of orange. This RGB model is the fundamental way computers represent color in digital images.
questions.question: What are the three color values that make up each pixel in a digital image?

questions.lessonContent: An HD screenshot with dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels total (2,073,600 pixels to be exact). Since each pixel needs 3 bytes of data—one byte for red, one for green, and one for blue—the raw uncompressed size is 6,220,800 bytes, which is approximately 6.2 megabytes. This calculation demonstrates why image compression is necessary: a single uncompressed HD image takes over 6 MB of storage. Without compression, the internet as we know it couldn't exist due to the massive amount of data that would need to be transmitted.
questions.question: A 1920 × 1080 pixel image has 2,073,600 pixels, and each pixel needs 3 bytes (one for red, green, and blue). The file size is approximately 6.2 MB. This statement about image data size is true.

questions.lessonTitle: The Three Tricks of Lossless Compression
questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression, used by formats like PNG, preserves every single pixel perfectly while still reducing file size. It accomplishes this using three distinct techniques applied in sequence. First, filtering (also called prediction) stores how each pixel differs from its neighbor rather than storing absolute values, since adjacent pixels are usually similar. Second, the LZ77 algorithm finds repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with compact back-references pointing to earlier occurrences. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently, similar to how Morse code uses short signals for common letters like 'E'. For a photograph, this pipeline can achieve approximately 3 times compression with zero quality loss.
questions.question: What are the three techniques that lossless compression (like PNG) uses to shrink file size while preserving all pixel data?
choices: Delta encoding, lossy transformation, and entropy coding
Quantization, DCT transformation, and color separation
Filtering (prediction), LZ77 (pattern finding), and Huffman coding
Run-length encoding, byte stuffing, and checksums
questions.explanation: The correct answer is filtering, LZ77, and Huffman coding. Filtering stores differences between adjacent pixels. LZ77 finds repeated patterns and replaces them with references. Huffman coding gives common values shorter binary codes.

questions.lessonContent: In PNG lossless compression, the process follows a specific sequence of techniques to reduce file size while preserving all pixel data. First, Apply Filtering is used to store differences between pixels rather than absolute values, making the data more predictable. Second, LZ77 Pattern Finding identifies repeated sequences in the filtered data and replaces them with compact back-references. Third, Huffman Encoding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values, further reducing the data size. This three-step sequence forms the core of PNG's lossless compression algorithm.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in PNG lossless compression?

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression exploits how human vision works to throw away data without noticeable quality loss. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together, meaning you notice blurry edges but won't notice if colors are slightly off. JPEG takes advantage of this by first converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color, then reducing color resolution since your eyes won't notice small color differences. The image is divided into 8×8 pixel blocks and each block is transformed into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most information ends up in just a few low-frequency components, allowing JPEG to throw away high-frequency details you won't miss.
questions.question: What two aspects of human vision does JPEG exploit for compression?

questions.lessonContent: When JPEG compresses an image, it divides each image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components using a mathematical process. Low-frequency components represent smooth gradients in the image, which appear as gradual color transitions in photographs. High-frequency components represent fine details like sharp edges, textures, and small objects. Since photographs primarily contain smooth gradients rather than sharp edges, most of the visually important information exists in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details that humans typically won't notice while keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: In JPEG compression, low-frequency components represent smooth gradients while high-frequency components represent fine details like sharp edges.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression offers significant file size reduction but with permanent data loss. At high quality settings, the difference between the original and compressed image is barely noticeable to the human eye. However, at very high compression levels, you will see blocking artifacts where fine details get lost and the image appears blocky or pixelated. Once JPEG throws away data during compression, you cannot get the original pixels back - this is the fundamental trade-off of lossy compression. Despite this limitation, the trade-off is often worth it because JPEG can achieve 10 to 20 times smaller file sizes with minimal visible difference to the average viewer.
questions.question: Which of the following describes the file size reduction and quality trade-off in JPEG compression?
choices: 5x smaller files with no quality loss
2-3x smaller files with no visible difference
50x smaller files with major visible artifacts
10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that JPEG achieves 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference, making this the correct answer.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression exploits how human vision works. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. First, it converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. It also reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice. Then it divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in JPEG lossy compression?

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses filtering (prediction) to compress images by storing differences between pixels rather than absolute values. The PNG standard defines four prediction methods that encoders can choose from per row. 'Sub' predicts each pixel from its left neighbor, which works best for horizontal gradients. 'Up' predicts from the pixel above, best for vertical gradients. 'Average' predicts from the average of the left and above pixels. 'Paeth' is a smarter method that calculates which neighbor (left, above, or diagonal) is closest in value and predicts from that one. PNG encoders test each method and select the one that produces the best compression for each row.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method works best for horizontal gradients?

questions.lessonContent: After prediction filtering, PNG uses the LZ77 algorithm to find and replace repeated patterns. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of processed data. When the algorithm encounters a sequence that matches something previously seen within this window, instead of storing the full sequence again, it writes a back-reference indicating how far back to look and how many bytes to copy. This is much more compact than repeating the same values. For images with large areas of similar color or gradual gradients, this technique significantly reduces file size by exploiting local repetition.
questions.question: In LZ77 compression, if the algorithm finds a sequence of 5 repeated values located 8 positions back in the data, it will store a reference pointing back 8 positions and copy 5 values, rather than storing the values themselves. This statement about LZ77 back-references is true.

questions.lessonContent: PNG files organize compressed data into structured chunks, each serving a specific purpose in the file format. The three essential chunks are IHDR (Image Header containing metadata like width, height, bit depth, and color type), IDAT (Image Data containing the actual compressed pixel information), and IEND (Image End marking the file's conclusion). Each chunk includes a CRC-32 checksum, which is a mathematical fingerprint of the chunk's data. When opening a PNG file, the computer recalculates this checksum to verify data integrity; if it doesn't match, the file is considered corrupted or damaged. This error detection mechanism protects against issues like network transmission errors or buggy programs.
questions.question: Which PNG chunk contains the compressed pixel data?
questions.explanation: IDAT is the Image Data chunk that contains the actual compressed pixel information. IHDR contains metadata like dimensions and bit depth, while IEND marks the end of the file. There is no separate CRC chunk; checksums are embedded within each chunk.

questions.lessonContent: The DEFLATE algorithm used in PNG compression combines two key techniques to shrink data. First, LZ77 scans for repeated patterns in the previous 32 KB of data and replaces them with compact back-references instead of storing the full values. After pattern-finding, some values appear much more frequently than others - for example, zero might appear 60% of the time. Huffman coding then assigns shorter binary codes to common values and longer codes to rare ones.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the DEFLATE algorithm used for PNG compression?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: There were two distinct periods of Roman government. The Roman Republic existed from 509 BCE to 30 BCE. The Roman Empire began in 30 BCE and lasted until 476 CE. Rome technically had an empire under the Roman Republic, but the term 'Roman Empire' specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus when Rome was ruled by emperors.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
questions.answer: Roman Republic: 509 BCE-30 BCE; Roman Empire: 30 BCE-476 CE

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate gave him the name Augustus, meaning 'most high.' In 23 BCE, Augustus was made consul for life by the Senate. He was also given the title 'Princeps,' meaning 'first citizen,' which is the origin of the word 'prince.' Additionally, he was made 'Imperator,' meaning 'successful general,' which is the origin of the word 'emperor.'
questions.question: The title 'Princeps' given to Augustus means 'first citizen' and is the origin of the word 'prince'.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, meaning Roman Peace, was a period when Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, establishing complete control that resulted in almost no warfare. This peace lasted nearly 200 years, making it one of the longest periods of peace in history. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship, extending the benefits of Roman membership throughout the empire.
questions.question: What was the Pax Romana?
choices: A period beginning in 27 BCE when Augustus conquered all of Italy
A period when the Roman Empire was divided into eastern and western halves
A period of nearly 200 years of peace when Rome controlled the Mediterranean region with almost no warfare
A period when Rome fought continuous wars to expand its territories
questions.explanation: The Pax Romana was a period of nearly 200 years of peace when Rome controlled the Mediterranean region with almost no warfare, beginning with Augustus and ending with Marcus Aurelius.

questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After the death of Emperor Nero in 68 CE, Rome experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. Four emperors ruled in quick succession during this period: Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and finally Vespasian. This illustrated the problems of imperial succession that had plagued the Roman Empire since Augustus. The military played an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor during this chaotic period. The Year of the Four Emperors demonstrated how the lack of a clear succession method could lead to instability and civil conflict.
questions.question: What was the Year of the Four Emperors?
questions.answer: A brief period of civil war after the death of Emperor Nero in 69 CE, during which four emperors (Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian) ruled in quick succession

questions.lessonContent: Gaius Caesar Germanicus, known as Caligula, was the son of the famed military leader Germanicus, who was the nephew and adopted son of Tiberius. Caligula earned his nickname "Caligula," meaning "little boots," from the Roman army as a child because he was dressed like a soldier. He became emperor in 37 CE and initially provided two years of good, effective rule. However, this was interrupted by a severe illness, followed by two years of terrible rule during which he exiled, killed, or forced suicide members of his own family and perceived enemies. Caligula was assassinated in 41 CE by members of the Praetorian Guard.
questions.question: Caligula was the son of the famous military leader Germanicus.

questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire saw many emperors with varying levels of success and achievement. Vespasian, who ruled from 69 to 79 CE, built the Colosseum in Rome, the famous arena where gladiatorial combats were held. Hadrian, who ruled from 117 to 138 CE, strengthened the empire's defenses by building Hadrian's Wall in Britannia, which separated Roman territory from the Picts in what is now Scotland. Trajan, who ruled from 98 to 117 CE, oversaw the expansion of the empire to its greatest extent and is considered to have been a great emperor. He launched massive public works programs in Rome including Trajan's Column, Trajan's Forum, and Trajan's Market.
questions.question: Which emperor built the Colosseum in Rome?
questions.explanation: Vespasian built the Colosseum in Rome as a place where gladiatorial combats were held. This was one of his major construction projects during his reign from 69 to 79 CE.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire officially ended in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian leader named Odoacer. This event marks the traditional end of ancient Rome and the beginning of the Middle Ages in Western Europe. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire, however, continued to exist for nearly another thousand years until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The fall of the Western Roman Empire was the result of multiple factors including economic troubles, military decline, political instability, and social problems.
questions.question: In what year did the Western Roman Empire officially end?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Division of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian first divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) in 285 CE, believing this would strengthen the empire for more effective administration. Once Constantine established Constantinople as a capital city, the split between east and west deepened considerably. The Western Roman Empire ended in 476 CE, while the Eastern Byzantine Empire lasted until 1453 when conquered by the Ottoman Turks. This means the Eastern Empire existed for nearly 1,000 years longer than the Western Empire.
questions.question: The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted longer than the Western Roman Empire.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: The Romans spoke Latin, from which the Romance languages developed. These include French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish. The English language also has significant Latin roots - about half of modern English can be traced to Latin, particularly after William the Conqueror brought French to England in 1066. Latin was also preserved by the Catholic Church, which continued using it for masses until the 1960s. Additionally, Latin became the traditional language for law, medicine, and science, with scientific names and most legal and medical terminology remaining in Latin.
questions.question: Which of the following languages developed from Latin?
questions.explanation: Spanish is a Romance language (Romance meaning 'Roman'), which developed directly from Latin along with French, Italian, Portuguese, and Romanian.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: The process of dividing and relocating the Roman Empire's political center involved several key transformations. First, Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE, creating separate East and West administrations. Later, Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, and renamed the city Constantinople. Once Constantinople was established as the capital city, the east/west split between the two empires deepened considerably.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the relocation of Rome's political center from Rome to Constantinople?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.moduleTitle: Foundations and Architecture of Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the entire research process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information before returning their findings to the lead agent. This architecture enables the system to handle complex, dynamic research tasks that would be impossible for a single linear pipeline.
questions.question: What architecture pattern does Anthropic's Research system use for coordinating multiple agents?

questions.moduleTitle: Foundations and Architecture of Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: In Anthropic's Research system, the lead agents execute subagents synchronously, meaning they wait for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This approach simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. The lead agent cannot steer subagents in real-time, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. Asynchronous execution would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed.
questions.question: In Anthropic's Research system, the lead agent executes subagents asynchronously to enable additional parallelism.

questions.moduleTitle: Foundations and Architecture of Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: When conducting long-horizon research conversations, the system must manage context carefully as standard context windows become insufficient. The LeadResearcher begins by thinking through its approach and saving its plan to Memory to persist the context. This is critical because if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens it will be truncated, losing important work. The system implements patterns where agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. When context limits approach, agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs and retrieving stored context like the research plan from memory.
questions.question: What happens when the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens in Anthropic's Research system?
choices: The system automatically creates new subagents
The lead agent restarts from the beginning
questions.explanation: The system explicitly saves the research plan to Memory because if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens it will be truncated, making it important to retain the plan for continuity.

questions.lessonTitle: Tool Description Optimization and Performance Gains
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic created a tool-testing agent that attempts to use flawed MCP tools and then rewrites their descriptions to prevent failures. This agent tests tools dozens of times to identify key nuances and bugs in the descriptions. The process of improving tool ergonomics resulted in a 40% decrease in task completion time for future agents using the new tool descriptions, because the improved descriptions helped agents avoid most mistakes. Bad tool descriptions can send agents down completely wrong paths, so each tool needs a distinct purpose and a clear description.
questions.question: What percentage decrease in task completion time did Anthropic achieve after their tool-testing agent rewrote flawed MCP tool descriptions?

questions.lessonContent: When a lead agent decomposes queries into subtasks for subagents, each subagent needs specific components to execute effectively. These requirements include an objective that defines what the subagent should accomplish, an output format specifying how results should be structured, guidance on which tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries that define what is included and excluded from the task. Anthropic found that without detailed task descriptions, agents would duplicate work, leave gaps in research, or fail to find necessary information. Early experiments with simple, short instructions led to vague interpretations where different subagents performed the exact same searches without effective division of labor.
questions.question: True or False: Anthropic found that giving subagents simple, short instructions without detailed task descriptions improved their coordination and reduced duplicate work.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic embedded explicit scaling rules in their prompts to help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently based on query complexity. For simple fact-finding tasks, the system uses just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls. Direct comparison queries might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 tool calls each. Complex research tasks that require thorough investigation may use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These guidelines were designed to prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions of the system.
questions.question: According to Anthropic's scaling rules embedded in prompts, how many subagents with how many tool calls each are recommended for direct comparison queries?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 2-4 subagents with 10-15 tool calls each, as explicitly stated in the source content for direct comparison queries. This distinguishes it from simple fact-finding (1 agent, 3-10 calls) and complex research (10+ subagents with divided responsibilities).

questions.lessonTitle: Early Evaluation Strategy with Small Samples
questions.lessonContent: In early agent development, changes tend to have dramatic impacts because there is abundant low-hanging fruit. A prompt tweak might boost success rates from 30% to 80%. With effect sizes this large, you can spot changes with just a few test cases. Anthropic started with a set of about 20 queries representing real usage patterns. Testing these queries often allowed them to clearly see the impact of changes. Many AI developer teams delay creating evals because they believe only large evals with hundreds of test cases are useful, but it is best to start with small-scale testing right away with a few examples rather than delaying until building more thorough evals.
questions.question: Approximately how many test queries did Anthropic use initially to evaluate their research agents?

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever Anthropic deploys updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. They need to prevent well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents, and cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, they use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to update their agent systems without disrupting running agents.

questions.lessonTitle: Evaluation Criteria for Research Agent Outputs
questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. LLMs are a natural fit for grading outputs. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (whether claims match sources), citation accuracy (whether cited sources match the claims), completeness (whether all requested aspects are covered), source quality (whether it used primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources), and tool efficiency (whether it used the right tools a reasonable number of times).
questions.question: Which evaluation criterion was resolved by adding source quality heuristics to the prompts when human testers noticed agents consistently chose SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative sources?
questions.explanation: Human testers noticed that early agents consistently chose SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative but less highly-ranked sources like academic PDFs or personal blogs, so source quality heuristics were added to the prompts to resolve this issue.

questions.lessonContent: The evaluation of research agents follows a specific progression from initial testing to refinement. We start by evaluating immediately with small samples, as changes in early agent development tend to have dramatic impacts because there is abundant low-hanging fruit. Once we have a small sample working, we test with about 20 queries representing real usage patterns to clearly see the impact of changes. After small-scale testing, we scale our evaluation using LLM-as-judge, which evaluates outputs against criteria like factual accuracy and citation accuracy. Human evaluation then catches what automation misses, such as hallucinated answers or subtle source selection biases. Finally, based on all evaluation findings, we refine prompts to address the identified issues.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the agent evaluation workflow for research systems?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released on January 11, 2024. It offers 8 leading embedding models, including top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. Additionally, the endpoint includes newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context handling. These models are available at competitive prices, being up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.
questions.question: How many leading embedding models are available in the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonTitle: Context Length Capability of M2-Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides state-of-the-art long context M2-Retrieval models. These models support context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens. The M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. This capability allows users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings.
questions.question: The M2-Retrieval models support context lengths up to 32k tokens.

questions.lessonTitle: Available Context Length Options for M2-BERT Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: The M2-BERT retrieval models are specifically designed for long context retrieval tasks. These models come in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k. The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model has an embedding dimension of 768. Users can select the appropriate model based on their specific use case requirements, with longer context models allowing for processing of more extensive documents in a single embedding generation call.
questions.question: What are the available context length options for M2-BERT retrieval models?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that M2-BERT retrieval models are available for long context with options of 2k, 8k, and 32k context length.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing developers who have already built applications following the OpenAI API to easily migrate. To configure the client for Together, you need to set the base_url parameter to "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" when initializing the OpenAI client. The API key is set using the Together API key. This compatibility means existing applications can switch to Together's service with minimal code changes, primarily by updating the base_url and API credentials.
